## To remember

- Table = rows (records / tuples) × columns (fields / attributes). **Schema** =
  the structure without data; **instance** = the content at one moment.
  Physical / logical / view schema = the three ANSI-SPARC levels.
- **ACID**: Atomicity (all or nothing — recovery subsystem, log, old values),
  Consistency (integrity constraints hold — the programmer), Isolation (no
  interference — concurrency control; anomalies: dirty write/read,
  non-repeatable read, phantom; relaxed via isolation levels), Durability
  (commits persist — recovery subsystem, log redo/undo after a crash).
- A **data model** = conceptual tools to describe data, relationships,
  semantics and constraints. Blocks: entity, entity set, attribute, constraint.
- Models: **hierarchical** (tree, one parent, 1:M), **network** (graph, several
  parents), **E-R** (high-level, visual, three parts), **relational** (tables =
  relations, the most common), **OO** (objects, OID references), **OR**
  (hybrid, foreign keys), **semi-structured** (schema and data mixed: XML,
  emails, web pages).
- E-R: **rectangle** = entity, **oval** = attribute, **diamond** = relationship.
  Key attribute **underlined**. Composite = sub-ovals; multi-valued = **double
  oval**; derived = **dashed oval**. Every entity needs a primary key.
  Descriptive attribute = attribute of a relationship. Binary = 2 entities,
  ternary = 3.

questions.question_text: Data in a database is typically organised into tables. What does one row represent?
questions.choice_a: A single attribute of the data
questions.choice_b: A single record or instance of data
questions.choice_c: The whole schema
questions.choice_d: An index
questions.explanation: Each row is one record / instance; each column is a specific attribute or characteristic of that data.

questions.question_text: What is a schema?
questions.choice_a: The data currently stored in the database
questions.choice_b: A description of a collection of data in a given data model — the structure or form of the database with no data in it
questions.choice_c: A backup copy of the database
questions.choice_d: A query written in SQL
questions.explanation: The schema is the definition of the structure; an instance is the actual content at a moment in time.

questions.question_text: At which schema level is the storage of data in blocks described?
questions.choice_a: View schema
questions.choice_b: Logical schema
questions.choice_c: Physical schema
questions.choice_d: External schema
questions.explanation: The physical schema describes how the data stored in blocks of storage is organised.

questions.question_text: Who works at the logical schema level?
questions.choice_a: End users only
questions.choice_b: Programmers and database administrators
questions.choice_c: The hardware vendor
questions.choice_d: Nobody; it is generated automatically
questions.explanation: At the logical level, data is described as record types stored in data structures; the internal implementation details are hidden here (they live at the physical level).

questions.question_text: The view schema generally describes:
questions.choice_a: How indexes are built
questions.choice_b: End-user interaction with the database system
questions.choice_c: The disk block size
questions.choice_d: The transaction log format
questions.explanation: Different views (also called the external schema) describe how particular users see the data; they are generated on demand from the real data.

questions.question_text: In the university-database example, 'Course_info(cid, enrollment)' is part of which schema?
questions.choice_a: The physical schema
questions.choice_b: The conceptual schema
questions.choice_c: An external schema (a view)
questions.choice_d: The internal schema
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema holds Students, Courses and Enrolled; the physical schema stores relations as unordered files with an index; Course_info is a view.

questions.question_text: What does the 'A' in ACID stand for, and what does it require?
questions.choice_a: Availability — the database is always online
questions.choice_b: Atomicity — a transaction is performed in its entirety or not at all
questions.choice_c: Authorization — only permitted users may write
questions.choice_d: Auditing — every change is logged for review
questions.explanation: Atomicity is ensured by the transaction-recovery subsystem, which must undo any effects of a failed (aborted) transaction, using the log to write back the old values.

questions.question_text: Which subsystem ensures atomicity by undoing a failed transaction's effects?
questions.choice_a: The concurrency-control subsystem
questions.choice_b: The transaction-recovery subsystem, using the log to write back old values
questions.choice_c: The query optimiser
questions.choice_d: The buffer manager
questions.explanation: Cooperation with the concurrency-control subsystem is also necessary.

questions.question_text: Consistency (the 'C' in ACID) is primarily the responsibility of:
questions.choice_a: The database program — that is, the programmer
questions.choice_b: The disk controller
questions.choice_c: The end user
questions.choice_d: The network layer
questions.explanation: Each transaction should bring the database from one consistent state (integrity constraints satisfied) to another; transactions may use abort instructions, leading to rollbacks handled by the recovery subsystem.

questions.question_text: Isolation is ensured by which subsystem?
questions.choice_a: The recovery subsystem
questions.choice_b: The concurrency-control subsystem
questions.choice_c: The DDL interpreter
questions.choice_d: The file manager
questions.explanation: Ideally we avoid all anomalies (dirty writes and reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms); because full isolation is expensive it is often relaxed via isolation levels.

questions.question_text: Why is full isolation often relaxed in practice?
questions.choice_a: It is illegal in some countries
questions.choice_b: It can be too expensive in terms of efficiency, so isolation levels trade some guarantees for speed
questions.choice_c: Modern hardware makes it unnecessary
questions.choice_d: Because atomicity already covers it
questions.explanation: Concurrency control is one of the most difficult and interesting issues in transaction management.

questions.question_text: Durability guarantees that:
questions.choice_a: The database never runs out of disk space
questions.choice_b: The changes of committed transactions must persist, even after a crash
questions.choice_c: Every transaction eventually commits
questions.choice_d: Uncommitted data is visible to all users
questions.explanation: After a crash the log is used to restore committed transactions and roll back uncommitted ones; the cache complicates the restoration.

questions.question_text: A data model is:
questions.choice_a: A physical layout of disk blocks
questions.choice_b: A collection of conceptual tools for describing data, data relationships, data semantics and consistency constraints
questions.choice_c: A specific SQL query
questions.choice_d: A backup strategy
questions.explanation: A data model provides a way to describe the design of a database; it is widely used in DBMSs to show how data is related, stored, retrieved and modified.

questions.question_text: In data-model terms, an 'entity' is:
questions.choice_a: A single column of a table
questions.choice_b: Anything about which data is to be collected and stored — a particular type of real-world object
questions.choice_c: A restriction placed on the data
questions.choice_d: A relationship between two tables
questions.explanation: A set of entities of the same type that share the same properties is an entity set; a characteristic of an entity is an attribute.

questions.question_text: What is a constraint, and why does it matter?
questions.choice_a: A synonym for an attribute
questions.choice_b: A restriction placed on the data; it helps ensure data integrity
questions.choice_c: The maximum number of rows in a table
questions.choice_d: The primary key of an entity
questions.explanation: Constraints are important because they help to ensure data integrity.

questions.question_text: Which relationship cardinalities does the course list?
questions.choice_a: 1:1, 1:M and M:N
questions.choice_b: Only 1:1 and M:N
questions.choice_d: Weak, strong and derived
questions.explanation: A relationship describes an association among entities; the types are one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many.

questions.question_text: The hierarchical model organises data as:
questions.choice_a: A set of two-dimensional tables
questions.choice_b: A tree-like structure with a single parent / root for each record, siblings in a set sequence
questions.choice_c: A graph where records can have several parents
questions.choice_d: A collection of objects
questions.explanation: It depicts a set of 1:M relationships between a parent and its children's segments.

questions.question_text: A stated disadvantage of the hierarchical model is that:
questions.choice_a: It is slow to traverse
questions.choice_b: It does not support complex relationships / more than one parent per child (so no M:N), and deleting a parent deletes its children
questions.choice_c: Changes in a parent are not reflected in children
questions.choice_d: It cannot store text
questions.explanation: Advantages: simple and fast to traverse; any change in the parent node is automatically reflected in the child, maintaining integrity.

questions.question_text: The network model differs from the hierarchical model mainly because:
questions.choice_a: It uses tables instead of a tree
questions.choice_b: A record can have several parents — it replaces the hierarchical tree with a graph
questions.choice_c: It has no relationships at all
questions.choice_d: It stores only numeric data
questions.explanation: It was the most prevalent model before the relational model; e.g. a Student node can have both a CSE Department parent and a Library parent.

questions.question_text: A disadvantage of the network model is that:
questions.choice_a: Data can only be reached by a single path
questions.choice_b: As more relationships are added the system becomes complex, and any update, deletion or insertion is quite difficult
questions.choice_c: It cannot maintain a parent-child relationship
questions.choice_d: It has no data integrity
questions.explanation: Advantage: because data is more linked and there may be more than one path to a node, information can be accessed in several ways, and the parent-child link gives integrity.

questions.question_text: The Entity-Relationship model is described as:
questions.choice_a: A low-level physical storage model
questions.choice_b: A high-level data-model diagram that expresses the real-world problem in visual form so stakeholders and developers can grasp the system
questions.choice_c: A query language
questions.choice_d: A backup format
questions.explanation: The ER diagram is the visual tool used to depict an ER model; it is made up of entities, attributes and relationships.

questions.question_text: A disadvantage of the Entity-Relationship model is:
questions.choice_a: It cannot be converted to the relational model
questions.choice_b: There is no industry standard for the notation, and some information may be hidden in the high-level view
questions.choice_c: It is conceptually very hard to build
questions.choice_d: It cannot represent relationships
questions.explanation: Advantages: conceptually simple, an effective communication tool, and it maps well to the relational model (and others).

questions.question_text: In the relational model, tables are also referred to as:
questions.choice_a: Segments
questions.choice_b: Relations
questions.choice_c: Objects
questions.choice_d: Nodes
questions.explanation: Data is kept as a two-dimensional table of rows and columns; tables (relations) are the foundation of the relational paradigm.

questions.question_text: 'Structural independence' in the relational model means:
questions.choice_a: The database has no structure
questions.choice_b: You can change the database structure without changing the way the data is accessed (the DBMS can still access the data)
questions.choice_c: Every table is independent and cannot be joined
questions.choice_d: The hardware is independent of the software
questions.explanation: Advantages of the relational model: simple, scalable (add rows and columns freely), and structural independence.

questions.question_text: A disadvantage of the relational model, per the course, is:
questions.choice_a: It cannot scale
questions.choice_b: Hardware overheads — hiding the complexity requires more powerful computers and storage — and its ease of design can lead to a poor database that slows down as it grows
questions.choice_c: It has no way to enforce integrity
questions.choice_d: It cannot represent 1:M relationships
questions.explanation: Because users need not know how data is stored, the ease of design can produce a bad schema.

questions.question_text: In the object-oriented (OO) data model, how are relationships represented?
questions.choice_a: By foreign-key attributes
questions.choice_b: By references via the object identifier (OID)
questions.choice_c: By a parent pointer in a tree
questions.choice_d: By a diamond symbol
questions.explanation: An OO database is a collection of objects (attributes + operations); OIDs are assigned automatically and it works well with OOP languages such as Java, C# and Swift.

questions.question_text: The object-relational (OR) model is:
questions.choice_a: A pure object database with no tables
questions.choice_b: A hybrid of the relational and object-oriented models, created to bridge the gap between them, allowing complex data types built on existing ones
questions.choice_c: An older name for the hierarchical model
questions.choice_d: A model with no schema
questions.explanation: The trade-off is that it may become complicated and difficult to manage, so a thorough understanding of it is essential.

questions.question_text: Which comparison of OO and OR databases is correct?
questions.choice_a: OO uses foreign keys; OR uses the OID
questions.choice_b: OO represents relationships by references via the OID and handles larger, more complex data but is less efficient; OR represents relationships by foreign keys and is comparatively more efficient
questions.choice_c: OO and OR are identical
questions.choice_d: OR handles more complex data than OO
questions.explanation: OR databases have data-manipulation languages such as SQL, QUEL and QBE based on relational calculus.

questions.question_text: The semi-structured model is characterised by:
questions.choice_a: A rigid, fixed schema for every entity
questions.choice_b: Data and schema that cannot be clearly told apart; some entities may miss attributes while others have extra ones
questions.choice_c: Storage only as two-dimensional tables
questions.choice_d: A single parent per record
questions.explanation: It emerged from the relational model and allows greater storage flexibility; examples include emails, XML and other markup languages, TCP/IP packets and web pages.

questions.question_text: Which is an example of a semi-structured data source?
questions.choice_a: A normalised SQL table
questions.choice_b: XML (and other markup languages), emails, web pages
questions.choice_c: A B-tree index
questions.choice_d: A transaction log
questions.explanation: In web-based data sources we often cannot distinguish the website's structure from its data.

questions.question_text: In an E-R diagram, an entity is represented by:
questions.choice_a: An oval
questions.choice_b: A diamond
questions.choice_c: A rectangle containing the entity name
questions.choice_d: An underlined word
questions.explanation: An entity is a person, a place or an object; examples in a college database: Student, Faculty, Course, Department, Result, Class, Subject.

questions.question_text: In an E-R diagram, an attribute is represented by:
questions.choice_a: A rectangle
questions.choice_b: An oval containing the attribute name, joined to its entity by a line
questions.choice_c: A diamond
questions.choice_d: A double line
questions.explanation: An attribute is a property or detail about an entity, e.g. RollNo, Student Name, Branch, Semester, Address for the Student entity.

questions.question_text: In an E-R diagram, a relationship is represented by:
questions.choice_a: A rectangle
questions.choice_b: An oval
questions.choice_c: A diamond containing the relationship's name, on the line between two entities
questions.choice_d: An arrow
questions.explanation: A relationship is an association (connection) between several entities; e.g. Student —Issue— Book.

questions.question_text: How is a primary-key attribute shown, and how many must an entity have?
questions.choice_a: Shown in a double oval; an entity may have several
questions.choice_b: Underlined; every entity must have exactly one primary-key attribute
questions.choice_c: Shown in bold; an entity has zero or one
questions.choice_d: Shown in a rectangle; an entity has exactly two
questions.explanation: Each and every entity must have one primary-key attribute (e.g. RollNo for Student, BookNo for Book).

questions.question_text: What is a composite attribute?
questions.choice_a: An attribute with more than one value
questions.choice_b: An attribute that can be divided into subparts, e.g. Name into first / middle / last, or Address into street / city
questions.choice_c: An attribute whose value is calculated from others
questions.choice_d: An attribute shared by two entities
questions.explanation: A simple attribute (e.g. RollNo, CPI) cannot be divided into subparts.

questions.question_text: Which pair correctly contrasts single-valued and multi-valued attributes?
questions.choice_a: RollNo is multi-valued; PhoneNo is single-valued
questions.choice_b: RollNo is single-valued (one value); PhoneNo / EmailID are multi-valued (a person may have several)
questions.choice_c: Both are always single-valued
questions.choice_d: Multi-valued attributes cannot be stored in a database
questions.explanation: A single-valued attribute has one value; a multi-valued attribute has more than one.

questions.question_text: What is a derived attribute?
questions.choice_a: An attribute stored manually in the database
questions.choice_b: An attribute whose value is derived or calculated from other attributes, e.g. Age from Birthdate and the current date
questions.choice_c: An attribute that belongs to a relationship
questions.choice_d: The primary key of a weak entity
questions.explanation: Birthdate is a stored attribute (entered manually); Age is derived from it.

questions.question_text: A descriptive attribute is:
questions.choice_a: An attribute that describes an entity in words
questions.choice_b: An attribute of the relationship (not of an entity), e.g. IssueDate on the Issue relationship between Student and Book
questions.choice_c: A synonym for a composite attribute
questions.choice_d: Any attribute written in a comment
questions.explanation: Attributes of the relationship are called descriptive attributes.

questions.question_text: A relationship between exactly two entities is called:
questions.choice_a: A unary relationship
questions.choice_b: A binary relationship
questions.choice_c: A ternary relationship
questions.choice_d: A composite relationship
questions.explanation: Student —Issue— Book is binary. A relationship between three entities (e.g. Faculty —Guide— Student with a Project) is ternary.

questions.question_text: A relationship between three entities is called:
questions.choice_a: A binary relationship
questions.choice_b: A ternary relationship
questions.choice_c: A triple key
questions.choice_d: A composite entity
questions.explanation: Example: Faculty and Student linked through a Guide relationship that also involves a Project entity.

questions.question_text: What is 'Database Design' as defined at the start of Lecture 4?
questions.choice_a: The act of writing SQL SELECT statements
questions.choice_b: A collection of processes that facilitate the designing, development, implementation and maintenance of enterprise database management systems
questions.choice_c: Choosing which disk to buy
questions.choice_d: Drawing the user interface
questions.explanation: An E-R diagram is one graphical tool used within that design process.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to draw the E-R diagram for a library, given the entities Student and Book.
steps: Draw a rectangle for each entity: Student and Book
Attach the attributes of each entity as ovals (Student: RollNo, Name, Branch, Sem; Book: BookNo, Name, Author, Price)
Underline one primary-key attribute per entity (RollNo for Student, BookNo for Book)
Add a diamond named 'Issue' on the line connecting Student and Book
Attach the descriptive attribute 'Issue Date' to the Issue relationship
Label the cardinality of the Issue relationship (e.g. 1:M)
exercises.explanation: Entities (rectangles) → attributes (ovals) → primary keys (underlined) → relationship (diamond) → descriptive attributes → cardinality.

exercises.prompt: Process flowchart (not an E-R diagram): the steps of E-R modelling, from a written description to a finished diagram.
exercises.hint: Mostly linear, with one decision 'Any many-to-many relationship?': yes -> resolve it with a linking entity; no -> continue. Both paths reach 'label the cardinalities'.

nodes.label: Attach attributes (ovals) and underline the primary key
Resolve M:N with a linking entity

exercises.explanation: Entities first, then their attributes and keys, then the relationships between them, then cardinality. A many-to-many relationship is usually resolved into a linking (junction) entity before the diagram is finished.

exercises.prompt: Decision flowchart (not an E-R diagram): classify a relationship between entities A and B as 1:1, 1:M or M:N.
exercises.hint: Two decisions. D1: 'Can one A relate to many B?'. D2 (asked on each branch): 'Can one B relate to many A?'. The four leaves are M:N, 1:M, 1:M and 1:1.

nodes.label: INPUT: a relationship between A and B
Can one A relate to many B ?
Can one B relate to many A ?
Can one B relate to many A ?

exercises.explanation: If both sides can link to many, the relationship is M:N; if exactly one side can link to many, it is 1:M; if neither can, it is 1:1.

exercises.prompt: Decision flowchart (not an E-R diagram): convert one E-R relationship R (between A and B) into relational tables.
exercises.hint: Decision 'Is R many-to-many?': yes -> new table with both primary keys. No -> decision 'Is R one-to-many?': yes -> foreign key on the 'many' side; no -> foreign key on either side (1:1).

nodes.label: INPUT: relationship R between A and B
Create a new table R with the primary keys of A and B as a composite key
Post the 'one' side's primary key as a foreign key in the 'many' side
Post either primary key as a foreign key in the other table (1:1)

exercises.explanation: M:N becomes its own table keyed on both entities' primary keys; 1:M puts the 'one' side's key as a foreign key on the 'many' side; 1:1 puts a foreign key on either side.

exercises.prompt: Which data model cannot represent a many-to-many relationship because each record may have only one parent?
exercises.explanation: The hierarchical model is a tree with a single parent per record; the network model lifted that restriction by allowing several parents.

exercises.prompt: In the ACID acronym, which property guarantees that the changes of a committed transaction survive a system crash?
exercises.explanation: Durability is ensured by the recovery subsystem; after a crash the log restores committed transactions and rolls back the uncommitted ones.

exercises.prompt: Draw the E-R diagram of the library system: a Student issues a Book, and the issue has a date.
exercises.hint: Rectangles for the two entities, ovals for their attributes (the primary key is a key attribute), a diamond for Issue, and the descriptive attribute Issue Date hanging off the diamond. Click a line to set its cardinality: 1 on the Student side, N on the Book side.
exercises.explanation: Entity = rectangle, attribute = oval, primary key = underlined oval, relationship = diamond. Issue Date belongs to the relationship, not to either entity: that is a descriptive attribute. One student issues many books, so the line reads 1 on the Student side and N on the Book side.

exercises.prompt: Draw the entity Student with one attribute of each kind: primary key, stored, derived and multi-valued.
exercises.hint: One rectangle and four ovals. RollNo is the key attribute (underlined), Birth Date a plain one, Age is derived (dashed oval) and Phone No multi-valued (double oval). No cardinality needed.
exercises.explanation: Age is computed from Birth Date and today's date, so it is a derived attribute (dashed oval). A person may have several numbers, so Phone No is multi-valued (double oval). Birth Date is entered and kept: a plain stored attribute.

exercises.prompt: Draw the ternary relationship Guide, linking Faculty, Student and Project, each with its primary key.
exercises.hint: Three rectangles, one diamond named Guide joined to all three, and one key attribute per entity. No cardinality needed.
exercises.explanation: A relationship joining three entities is ternary. Each entity keeps exactly one primary-key attribute; the single Guide diamond carries all three lines rather than three separate binary relationships.

exercises.prompt: On this diagram, which attribute is derived?
exercises.explanation: The dashed oval marks a derived attribute: Age is computed from Birth Date and today's date, it is not stored.

exercises.prompt: On this diagram, which attribute is multi-valued?
exercises.explanation: The double oval marks a multi-valued attribute: a student may have several phone numbers.

exercises.prompt: On this diagram, which attribute is the primary key of Student?
exercises.explanation: The key attribute is the one whose name is underlined.

exercises.prompt: On this diagram, which attribute is a descriptive attribute?
exercises.explanation: Issue Date hangs off the relationship diamond, not off an entity: it describes the Issue relationship itself.

exercises.prompt: How many entities and how many relationships does this diagram contain?
exercises.explanation: Rectangles are entities (Student, Book), the diamond is the relationship (Issue); ovals are attributes, not entities.

name: Week 2
lesson:
# Software Engineering — Week 2

Software processes; the semester project; vision and prototype.

## SEMESTER PROJECT
- semester project = build one useful app or website around a real problem and a specific user
- project method = build a small version, then improve it with evidence
- project scope = test changes, learn to release and maintain it
- product-like project = no external customer gives a complete contract; the team chooses the target user, the features, and what evidence is convincing
- freedom creates product responsibility = the team must decide, not just execute a spec
- vague idea = produces arbitrary features
- vision = gives the team a basis for saying yes, no, or not yet

## TEAM
- team size = 2–3 members who can meet and communicate
- team record = names, a contact channel, a meeting time
- facilitator = role: runs the session
- recorder = role: writes things down
- speaker = role: presents the draft
- role rotation = combine roles with two members; rotate roles later

## PROGRAMMING vs SOFTWARE ENGINEERING
- programming = can you make it work?
- software engineering = can your team build it, test it, maintain it, and improve it?
- QuickCampus = fictional teaching case: an app that shipped every feature and still failed
- QuickCampus goal = help students find useful campus spaces and activities
- QuickCampus launch = rooms, events, chat, attendance, maps, AI recommendations
- QuickCampus result = stale data, a broken dependency, slow screens, one-star reviews

## SOFTWARE PROCESS
- software process = activities that produce a software product
- process activities = specification, design and implementation, validation, evolution
- plan-driven development = activities planned in advance; progress measured against the plan
- agile development = incremental; planning interleaved with the work; change expected
- Scrum = agile method: fixed-length sprints, product backlog, sprint backlog, daily stand-up, review, retrospective
- Scrum roles = product owner, scrum master, team
- Kanban = agile method: visualize the workflow on a board, limit work in progress (WIP), pull the next item; no fixed iterations
- teamwork = plan-driven and agile both depend on a team that communicates

## VISION — WHAT, WHO, WHY
- vision questions = What, Who, Why (Sommerville, Engineering Software Products, §1.1)
- What = what product are we proposing? what is its boundary?
- Who = who has the problem, in a specific situation?
- Why = what valuable outcome makes it worth choosing?
- hidden-decision words = "everyone", "all-in-one", "easy" usually hide decisions not yet made
- one-sentence vision = "We help [user] do [task] in [situation]"

## EXAMPLE — FINDING A MEETING TIME
- user and problem = student project teams lose time comparing availability in chat messages
- first version = enter available times, show the overlap
- outside the first version = chat and calendar integration
- assumption to test = teams will use it to choose a time

## FIRST VERSION AND BOUNDARY
- first version = one main task, up to three features
- current workaround = what users do today
- boundary = one feature deliberately left out for now
- goal = a useful, testable version the team can finish

## PROTOTYPE
- prototype purpose = make a risky assumption tangible
- prototype chain = risky assumption → small prototype → observable evidence (Sommerville §1.3)
- prototype rule = build only enough to learn whether the idea, interaction or technology is plausible
- example test plan = ask two classmates to find a shared time using the sketch; if either needs help, revise the flow and try again

## KEEP IMPROVING THE SAME PRODUCT
- weeks 2–4 = define the problem and requirements
- weeks 5–7 = build a small working version and check it
- week 8 = midterm examination
- weeks 9–12 = test, refactor, deploy, practise recovery
- weeks 13–15 = complete acceptance checks and show changes
- evidence to keep = user feedback, test results, change history (kept continuously, not reconstructed at the end)

## MILESTONE 1
- before leaving class = show one team worksheet; every member can explain the idea and the next test
- after class = complete M1: vision, assumptions, prototype plan, and an AI decision log

questions.question_text: According to Week 2, what is the difference between programming and software engineering?
questions.choice_a: Programming uses Python; software engineering uses Java
questions.choice_b: Programming asks 'can you make it work?'; software engineering asks 'can your team build it, test it, maintain it, and improve it?'
questions.choice_c: Programming is done alone; software engineering is done by a manager
questions.choice_d: There is no difference
questions.explanation: Software engineering is the disciplined development and evolution of software that must satisfy real stakeholder needs under constraints of time, cost, quality, security and change.

questions.question_text: What lesson does the QuickCampus teaching case illustrate?
questions.choice_a: You should always add more features
questions.choice_b: A team can ship and demo every feature and still fail — stale data, a broken dependency, slow screens, one-star reviews
questions.choice_c: AI recommendations guarantee success
questions.choice_d: Campus apps are impossible to build
questions.explanation: QuickCampus is a fictional teaching case: most screens opened and every feature could be demoed, yet the product failed in use.

questions.question_text: What are the four activities of a software process?
questions.choice_a: Planning, coding, meetings, shipping
questions.choice_b: Specification, design and implementation, validation, evolution
questions.choice_c: Design, test, deploy, delete
questions.choice_d: Requirements, UML, database, UI
questions.explanation: Every software process includes these activities in some form; processes differ in how they organise and sequence them.

questions.question_text: Plan-driven development is best described as:
questions.choice_a: Activities planned in advance, with progress measured against the plan
questions.choice_b: No planning at all
questions.choice_c: Planning only after the software ships
questions.choice_d: Planning done exclusively by the customer
questions.explanation: Plan-driven processes are predictable and well documented but make change costly to accommodate.

questions.question_text: Agile development differs from plan-driven development because:
questions.choice_a: It forbids all documentation
questions.choice_b: It is incremental, interleaves planning with the work, and expects change
questions.choice_c: It has no testing
questions.choice_d: It requires a fixed contract before any work starts
questions.explanation: Agile methods such as Scrum and Kanban accept that requirements will evolve during the project.

questions.question_text: In Scrum, work is organised into:
questions.choice_a: Unbounded phases
questions.choice_b: Fixed-length sprints, with a product backlog and a sprint backlog, a daily stand-up, and a review and retrospective each sprint
questions.choice_c: One long release at the end
questions.choice_d: Kanban columns with WIP limits
questions.explanation: Scrum roles include the product owner, the scrum master and the team.

questions.question_text: The defining practice of Kanban is:
questions.choice_a: Fixed two-week iterations
questions.choice_b: Visualising the workflow on a board and limiting work in progress (WIP), pulling the next item only when there is capacity
questions.choice_c: Writing a detailed plan up front
questions.choice_d: A daily stand-up meeting
questions.explanation: Unlike Scrum, Kanban has no fixed iterations; flow is controlled by WIP limits.

questions.question_text: Why is the semester project called 'product-like' rather than 'project-like'?
questions.choice_a: Because it must be sold for money
questions.choice_b: Because no external customer gives a complete contract — the team chooses the target user, the features, and what evidence is convincing
questions.choice_c: Because it has no deadline
questions.choice_d: Because it is built by one person
questions.explanation: Freedom creates product responsibility: the team must decide, not just execute a given spec.

questions.question_text: The slides say a vague idea produces arbitrary features, whereas a vision gives the team:
questions.choice_a: A guarantee of a good grade
questions.choice_b: A basis for saying yes, no, or not yet to proposed features
questions.choice_c: A fixed list of requirements from the professor
questions.choice_d: Permission to skip testing
questions.explanation: A vision is the reference the team checks each proposed feature against.

questions.question_text: A product vision answers which three questions?
questions.choice_a: When, Where, How much
questions.choice_b: What, Who, Why
questions.choice_c: Who, How, When
questions.choice_d: What, How, How much
questions.explanation: What: the product and its boundary. Who: who has the problem, in a specific situation. Why: the valuable outcome that makes it worth choosing. (Sommerville §1.1)

questions.question_text: Why do the words 'everyone', 'all-in-one' and 'easy' get flagged in a vision statement?
questions.choice_a: They are grammatically incorrect
questions.choice_b: They usually hide decisions the team has not made yet
questions.choice_c: They are trademarked
questions.choice_d: They make the vision too long
questions.explanation: A useful vision names a specific user, a bounded product and a concrete outcome instead of these catch-alls.

questions.question_text: Which sentence form does Week 2 give for a first-version vision?
questions.choice_a: 'This app will change the world.'
questions.choice_b: 'We help [user] do [task] in [situation].'
questions.choice_c: 'Our product is better than the competition.'
questions.choice_d: 'Everyone can use this easily.'
questions.explanation: Naming the user, the task and the situation forces the concrete decisions a vision needs.

questions.question_text: What should a 'first version' contain?
questions.choice_a: Every feature the team can imagine
questions.choice_b: One main task and up to about three features, with one feature explicitly left out as a boundary
questions.choice_c: Only a written report, no software
questions.choice_d: At least ten screens
questions.explanation: Also state the current workaround (what users do today) and aim for something useful, testable and finishable.

questions.question_text: In the meeting-time example, which is named as being *outside* the first version?
questions.choice_a: Entering your available times
questions.choice_b: Showing the overlap of available times
questions.choice_c: Chat and calendar integration
questions.choice_d: Choosing a meeting time
questions.explanation: The first version is: enter available times, show the overlap. The assumption to test is that teams will use it to choose a time.

questions.question_text: A prototype, in Week 2's sense, is used to:
questions.choice_a: Deliver the finished product early
questions.choice_b: Make a risky assumption tangible: build only enough to learn whether the idea, interaction or technology is plausible, and get observable evidence
questions.choice_c: Replace all testing
questions.choice_d: Impress the customer with polish
questions.explanation: The chain is: risky assumption → small prototype → observable evidence. (Sommerville §1.3)

questions.question_text: Which sequence describes the prototype loop from the slides?
questions.choice_a: Observable evidence → risky assumption → small prototype
questions.choice_b: Risky assumption → small prototype → observable evidence
questions.choice_c: Small prototype → risky assumption → observable evidence
questions.choice_d: Risky assumption → observable evidence → small prototype
questions.explanation: You start from the assumption most likely to sink the idea, build the smallest thing that tests it, and look at what actually happens.

questions.question_text: Over the semester, the teams are told to:
questions.choice_a: Switch to a new product idea every few weeks
questions.choice_b: Keep improving the same product: weeks 2–4 define the problem, 5–7 build and check a small version, 9–12 test / refactor / deploy, 13–15 acceptance checks
questions.choice_c: Build the whole product in the last week
questions.choice_d: Work individually and merge at the end
questions.explanation: Week 8 is the midterm examination. Evidence — feedback, test results, change history — is kept continuously.

questions.question_text: What does 'keep evidence' mean in this course?
questions.choice_a: Keep the source code only
questions.choice_b: Continuously keep user feedback, test results and change history, rather than reconstructing them at the end of the semester
questions.choice_c: Keep a copy of every email
questions.choice_d: Keep the professor's slides
questions.explanation: Team-project scores can be adjusted using contribution evidence: repository history, issue ownership, review activity, milestone check-ins.

questions.question_text: At the end of the Week 2 class, before leaving, each team must be able to:
questions.choice_a: Demo a working release
questions.choice_b: Show one team worksheet, with every member able to explain the idea and the next test
questions.choice_c: Submit the final report
questions.choice_d: Deploy to production
questions.explanation: After class the team completes Milestone 1 (vision, assumptions, prototype plan, and an AI decision log).

exercises.prompt: Order the Week-2 studio steps that take a team from a blank page to a first-version draft.
steps: Brainstorm problems you notice (who has it, when, how they handle it today)
Choose one problem the team can reach, build for, and observe
Write the one-sentence vision: 'We help [user] do [task] in [situation]'
Define the first version: one main task and up to three features
Name one boundary: a feature left out for now
Sketch two rough screens for the main task and name one assumption to test
exercises.explanation: Problems → pick one → vision sentence → first version → boundary → sketch + assumption. The output is one worksheet every member can explain.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart of using a prototype to test a risky assumption, looping until the evidence supports it.
exercises.hint: Decision 'Does the evidence support the assumption?': yes -> keep the idea, move to the first version, END; no -> revise the idea or flow, then loop back to building the prototype.

nodes.label: Build the smallest prototype that tests it
Put it in front of a real user and observe
Does the evidence support the assumption ?
Keep the idea, move to the first version
Revise the idea or the flow

exercises.explanation: Build only enough to learn; if the observable evidence does not support the assumption, revise and test again rather than proceeding to build the product.

exercises.prompt: Which agile method controls flow by visualising work on a board and limiting work in progress, with no fixed iterations?
exercises.explanation: Scrum uses fixed-length sprints; Kanban uses a board plus WIP limits and pull.

name: Vocabulaire
lesson:
# Vocabulaire coréen

## Pronoms

- 나 = na = [na] = je / moi (familier)
- 저 = jeo = [tjo] = je / moi (poli)
- 저는 = jeo-neun = [tjo-nen] = je... (avec particule de thème)
- 너 = neo = [no] = tu (familier)
- 우리 = u-ri = [ou-ri] = nous / notre
- 제 = je = [tjé] = mon (poli)
- 내 = nae = [nè] = mon (familier)

## Verbes

- 하다 = ha-da = [ha-da] = faire
- 있다 = it-da = [it-ta] = être / y avoir / avoir
- 없다 = eop-da = [op-ta] = ne pas être / ne pas avoir
- 가다 = ga-da = [ka-da] = aller
- 오다 = o-da = [o-da] = venir
- 보다 = bo-da = [po-da] = voir / regarder
- 먹다 = meok-da = [mok-ta] = manger
- 마시다 = ma-si-da = [ma-chi-da] = boire
- 좋아하다 = jo-a-ha-da = [tjo-a-ha-da] = aimer
- 필요하다 = pi-ryo-ha-da = [phi-ryo-ha-da] = avoir besoin
- 주다 = ju-da = [tjou-da] = donner
- 받다 = bat-da = [pat-ta] = recevoir
- 배고프다 = bae-go-peu-da = [pè-go-phe-da] = avoir faim
- 생각하다 = saeng-gak-ha-da = [sèng-gak-ha-da] = penser
- 쓰다 = sseu-da = [sse-da] = écrire / utiliser

## Adjectifs

- 좋다 = jo-ta = [tjo-tha] = être bien / aimer
- 작다 = jak-da = [tjak-ta] = être petit
- 많다 = man-ta = [man-tha] = y avoir beaucoup / être nombreux
- 적다 = jeok-da = [tjok-ta] = y avoir peu

lesson:
# Hangeul — lire et prononcer

Chaque case donne la syllabe puis, entre crochets, sa **phonétique approximative
à la française**. Ce n'est pas de l'API : c'est une béquille pour savoir quoi
dire à voix haute.

Format utilisé partout dans l'appli :
**맥주 = maek-ju = [mèk-tjou] → bière**

## Conventions

| Série | Lettres | Phonétique FR | Exemple |
|---|---|---|---|
| non aspirée | ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅈ | **k · t · p · tj** en tête de mot | 가 [ka] · 다 [ta] |
| non aspirée entre deux sonores | ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅈ | **g · d · b · dj** | 사과 = sa-gwa = [sa-gwa] |
| aspirée (souffle) | ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ | **kh · th · ph · tch** | 카 [kha] · 차 [tcha] |
| tendue (pincée) | ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ | **kk · tt · pp · ss · ttj** | 까 [kka] · 빠 [ppa] |

Voyelles à retenir : **ㅜ = ou**, **ㅡ = e** (comme dans « je »), **ㅓ = o**
ouvert, **ㅐ = è**, **ㅔ = é**, **ㅢ = eui**.

## Consonnes (자음)

| Lettre | RR | Phon. FR en tête | Phon. FR en batchim | Exemple |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ㄱ | g / k | k · g entre sonores | k | 가구 = ga-gu = [ka-gou] |
| ㄲ | kk | kk | k | 꼬리 = kko-ri = [kko-ri] |
| ㅋ | k | kh | k | 커피 = keo-pi = [kho-phi] |
| ㄴ | n | n | n | 나라 = na-ra = [na-ra] |
| ㄷ | d / t | t · d entre sonores | t | 다리 = da-ri = [ta-ri] |
| ㄸ | tt | tt | — | 머리띠 = meo-ri-tti = [mo-ri-tti] |
| ㅌ | t | th | t | 토마토 = to-ma-to = [tho-ma-tho] |
| ㄹ | r / l | r | l | 라디오 = ra-di-o = [ra-di-o] |
| ㅁ | m | m | m | 머리 = meo-ri = [mo-ri] |
| ㅂ | b / p | p · b entre sonores | p | 바나나 = ba-na-na = [pa-na-na] |
| ㅃ | pp | pp | — | 아빠 = a-ppa = [a-ppa] |
| ㅍ | p | ph | p | 포도 = po-do = [pho-do] |
| ㅅ | s | s · ch devant i/y | t | 사과 = sa-gwa = [sa-gwa] |
| ㅆ | ss | ss | t | 쓰다 = sseu-da = [sse-da] |
| ㅇ | — / ng | muette en tête | ng | 아이 = a-i = [a-i] |
| ㅈ | j | tj · dj entre sonores | t | 의자 = ui-ja = [eui-dja] |
| ㅉ | jj | ttj | — | 짜다 = jja-da = [ttja-da] |
| ㅊ | ch | tch | t | 기차 = gi-cha = [ki-tcha] |
| ㅎ | h | h (souvent effacé) | t | 호수 = ho-su = [ho-sou] |

## Voyelles (모음)

| Lettre | RR | Phon. FR | Lue seule (avec ㅇ) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ㅏ | a | a | 아 [a] |
| ㅐ | ae | è | 애 [è] |
| ㅑ | ya | ya | 야 [ya] |
| ㅒ | yae | yè | 얘 [yè] |
| ㅓ | eo | o | 어 [o] |
| ㅔ | e | é | 에 [é] |
| ㅕ | yeo | yo | 여 [yo] |
| ㅖ | ye | yé | 예 [yé] |
| ㅗ | o | o | 오 [o] |
| ㅘ | wa | wa | 와 [wa] |
| ㅙ | wae | wè | 왜 [wè] |
| ㅚ | oe | wé | 외 [wé] |
| ㅛ | yo | yo | 요 [yo] |
| ㅜ | u | ou | 우 [ou] |
| ㅝ | wo | wo | 워 [wo] |
| ㅞ | we | wé | 웨 [wé] |
| ㅟ | wi | wi | 위 [wi] |
| ㅠ | yu | you | 유 [you] |
| ㅡ | eu | e | 으 [e] |
| ㅢ | ui | eui | 의 [eui] |
| ㅣ | i | i | 이 [i] |

## Batchim — les 7 sons

Une consonne en fin de syllabe ne se prononce qu'en sept sons, **bloqués**
(la bouche prend la position mais ne libère pas l'air).

| Son | Lettres | Phon. FR | Exemple |
|---|---|---|---|
| [k] | ㄱ ㅋ ㄲ | k | 부엌 = bu-eok = [pou-ok] |
| [n] | ㄴ | n | 산 = san = [san] |
| [t] | ㄷ ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ ㅎ | t | 옷 = ot = [ot] |
| [l] | ㄹ | l | 물 = mul = [moul] |
| [m] | ㅁ | m | 봄 = bom = [pom] |
| [p] | ㅂ ㅍ | p | 앞 = ap = [ap] |
| [ng] | ㅇ | ng | 강 = gang = [kang] |

## Exemples

- 맥주 = maek-ju = [mèk-tjou] → **bière**
- 커피 = keo-pi = [kho-phi] → **café**
- 김치 = gim-chi = [kim-tchi] → **kimchi**
- 학교 = hak-gyo = [hak-kyo] → **école**
- 친구 = chin-gu = [tchin-gou] → **ami(e)**
- 사과 = sa-gwa = [sa-gwa] → **pomme**
- 물 = mul = [moul] → **eau**
- 안녕하세요 = an-nyeong-ha-se-yo = [an-nyong-ha-sé-yo] → **bonjour**
- 감사합니다 = gam-sa-ham-ni-da = [kam-sa-ham-ni-da] → **merci**
- 병원 = byeong-won = [pyong-won] → **hôpital**

lesson:
# Coréen — Semaine 1

Cours GEE3003 « Basic Korean », Day 1 (week_1.pdf) : les voyelles et les
consonnes de base, et la lecture de premiers mots.

## Voyelles de base (모음)

- ㅏ = a
- ㅑ = ya
- ㅓ = eo
- ㅕ = yeo
- ㅗ = o
- ㅛ = yo
- ㅜ = u
- ㅠ = yu
- ㅡ = eu
- ㅣ = i

Un trait court ajouté à ㅣ ou ㅡ donne ㅏ ㅓ ㅗ ㅜ ; un second trait donne les
voyelles iotisées ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ. Lues seules (avec la consonne muette ㅇ) :

|  | ㅏ | ㅑ | ㅓ | ㅕ | ㅗ | ㅛ | ㅜ | ㅠ | ㅡ | ㅣ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ㅇ** | 아 | 야 | 어 | 여 | 오 | 요 | 우 | 유 | 으 | 이 |

## Consonnes de base (자음)

- ㄱ = g / k
- ㄴ = n
- ㄷ = d / t
- ㄹ = r / l
- ㅁ = m
- ㅂ = b / p
- ㅅ = s
- ㅇ = muette en tête de syllabe, « ng » en finale
- ㅈ = j
- ㅎ = h

## Syllabes — consonne + voyelle

|  | ㅏ | ㅑ | ㅓ | ㅕ | ㅗ | ㅛ | ㅜ | ㅠ | ㅡ | ㅣ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ㄱ** | 가 | 갸 | 거 | 겨 | 고 | 교 | 구 | 규 | 그 | 기 |
| **ㄴ** | 나 | 냐 | 너 | 녀 | 노 | 뇨 | 누 | 뉴 | 느 | 니 |
| **ㄷ** | 다 | 댜 | 더 | 뎌 | 도 | 됴 | 두 | 듀 | 드 | 디 |
| **ㄹ** | 라 | 랴 | 러 | 려 | 로 | 료 | 루 | 류 | 르 | 리 |
| **ㅁ** | 마 | 먀 | 머 | 며 | 모 | 묘 | 무 | 뮤 | 므 | 미 |
| **ㅂ** | 바 | 뱌 | 버 | 벼 | 보 | 뵤 | 부 | 뷰 | 브 | 비 |
| **ㅅ** | 사 | 샤 | 서 | 셔 | 소 | 쇼 | 수 | 슈 | 스 | 시 |
| **ㅇ** | 아 | 야 | 어 | 여 | 오 | 요 | 우 | 유 | 으 | 이 |
| **ㅈ** | 자 | 쟈 | 저 | 져 | 조 | 죠 | 주 | 쥬 | 즈 | 지 |
| **ㅎ** | 하 | 햐 | 허 | 혀 | 호 | 효 | 후 | 휴 | 흐 | 히 |

## Mots (단어)

- dent = 이 = i
- enfant = 아이 = a-i
- cinq = 오 = o
- concombre = 오이 = o-i
- lait = 우유 = u-yu
- renard = 여우 = yeo-u
- meuble = 가구 = ga-gu
- papillon = 나비 = na-bi
- banane = 바나나 = ba-na-na
- chanteur / chanteuse = 가수 = ga-su
- bébé = 아기 = a-gi
- radio = 라디오 = ra-di-o
- viande = 고기 = go-gi
- chaussures = 구두 = gu-du
- grande sœur (d'un homme) = 누나 = nu-na

- cuisine / plat = 요리 = yo-ri

name: Semaine 2
lesson:
# Coréen — Semaine 2

Cours GEE3003 « Basic Korean », Day 2 (week_2.pdf) : consonnes aspirées et
tendues, voyelles composées, et les consonnes finales (받침).

## Consonnes aspirées (거센소리)

- ㅊ = ch
- ㅋ = k
- ㅌ = t
- ㅍ = p

|  | ㅏ | ㅑ | ㅓ | ㅕ | ㅗ | ㅛ | ㅜ | ㅠ | ㅡ | ㅣ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ㅊ** | 차 | 챠 | 처 | 쳐 | 초 | 쵸 | 추 | 츄 | 츠 | 치 |
| **ㅋ** | 카 | 캬 | 커 | 켜 | 코 | 쿄 | 쿠 | 큐 | 크 | 키 |
| **ㅌ** | 타 | 탸 | 터 | 텨 | 토 | 툐 | 투 | 튜 | 트 | 티 |
| **ㅍ** | 파 | 퍄 | 퍼 | 펴 | 포 | 표 | 푸 | 퓨 | 프 | 피 |

## Consonnes tendues (된소리)

- ㄲ = kk
- ㄸ = tt
- ㅃ = pp
- ㅆ = ss
- ㅉ = jj

|  | ㅏ | ㅓ | ㅗ | ㅜ | ㅡ | ㅣ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ㄲ** | 까 | 꺼 | 꼬 | 꾸 | 끄 | 끼 |
| **ㄸ** | 따 | 떠 | 또 | 뚜 | 뜨 | 띠 |
| **ㅃ** | 빠 | 뻐 | 뽀 | 뿌 | 쁘 | 삐 |
| **ㅆ** | 싸 | 써 | 쏘 | 쑤 | 쓰 | 씨 |
| **ㅉ** | 짜 | 쩌 | 쪼 | 쭈 | 쯔 | 찌 |

## Plaine / tendue / aspirée

| plaine | tendue | aspirée |
|---|---|---|
| 가 ga | 까 kka | 카 ka |
| 다 da | 따 tta | 타 ta |
| 바 ba | 빠 ppa | 파 pa |
| 사 sa | 싸 ssa | — |
| 자 ja | 짜 jja | 차 cha |

## Voyelles composées (모음 2)

- ㅐ = ae
- ㅒ = yae
- ㅔ = e
- ㅖ = ye
- ㅘ = wa
- ㅝ = wo
- ㅚ = oe
- ㅙ = wae
- ㅞ = we
- ㅟ = wi
- ㅢ = ui

Lues seules (avec ㅇ) : 애 얘 에 예 와 워 외 왜 웨 위 의.

## Consonnes finales — 받침

Une consonne en fin de syllabe ne se prononce qu'en 7 sons :

- [k] : ㄱ, ㅋ, ㄲ
- [n] : ㄴ
- [t] : ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ, ㅎ
- [l] : ㄹ
- [m] : ㅁ
- [p] : ㅂ, ㅍ
- [ng] : ㅇ

## Mots (단어)

### Consonnes aspirées

- jupe = 치마 = chi-ma
- café = 커피 = keo-pi
- train = 기차 = gi-cha
- nez = 코 = ko
- raisin = 포도 = po-do
- tomate = 토마토 = to-ma-to

### Consonnes tendues

- queue (d'animal) = 꼬리 = kko-ri
- lapin = 토끼 = to-kki
- serre-tête = 머리띠 = meo-ri-tti
- papa = 아빠 = a-ppa
- écrire = 쓰다 = sseu-da
- être salé = 짜다 = jja-da

### Voyelles composées

- montre / horloge = 시계 = si-gye
- chaise = 의자 = ui-ja
- magasin = 가게 = ga-ge
- gâteau sec = 과자 = gwa-ja
- oreille = 귀 = gwi
- serveur = 웨이터 = we-i-teo
- cochon = 돼지 = dwae-ji
- entreprise = 회사 = hoe-sa
- il fait froid = 추워요 = chu-wo-yo
- pourquoi = 왜 = wae
- chanson = 노래 = no-rae
- histoire / conversation = 얘기 = yae-gi

### 받침

- médicament = 약 = yak
- livre = 책 = chaek

name: Week 3
lesson:
# Computer Programming — Week 3

Chapter 3, *Constants, Variables, Data Type*. How C names and stores a value:
what type it has, how long it lives, and what "empty" means for it.

---

## 1. Primary data types

| category | types |
|---|---|
| **Integral — integer** | `int`, `short int`, `long int` (each `signed` by default, or `unsigned`) |
| **Integral — character** | `char`, `signed char`, `unsigned char` |
| **Floating point** | `float`, `double`, `long double` |
| **Other** | `void` |

Size and range depend on the machine word, but the slides give both:

| type | 16-bit machine | 32-bit machine (widely used) |
|---|---|---|
| `char` | 8 bits, -128 ~ 127 | 8 bits, -128 ~ 127 |
| `int` | 16 bits, -32,768 ~ 32,767 | 32 bits, -2,147,483,648 ~ 2,147,483,647 |
| `unsigned int` | 16 bits, 0 ~ 65,536 | 32 bits, 0 ~ 4,294,967,295 |
| `short int` | 8 bits, -128 ~ 127 | 16 bits, -32,768 ~ 32,767 |
| `long int` | 32 bits, -2,147,483 ~ 2,147,483,647 | 32 bits, same range |

| type | size (bits) | range / precision |
|---|---|---|
| `float` | 32 | ~3.4E-38 ~ 3.4E+38, 6 digits of precision |
| `double` | 64 | ~1.7E-308 ~ 1.7E+308, 14 digits of precision |
| `long double` | 80 | ~3.4E-4932 ~ 1.1E+4932 |

## 2. Declaring variables

```c
float x, y;
int code;
short int count;
long int amount;
double deviation;
unsigned n, m;
char c, d;
```

**Default type of a literal constant:**

| literal | type | why |
|---|---|---|
| `+111`, `-222` | `int` | integer constant, no suffix |
| `45678U` | `unsigned int` | `U` suffix |
| `-56789L` | `long int` | `L` suffix |
| `987654UL` | `unsigned long int` | `UL` suffix |
| `0.`, `.0`, `12.0`, `1.234` | `double` | floating constant, no suffix |
| `-1.2f` | `float` | `f` suffix |
| `1.23456789` (long) | `long double` | context/suffix dependent |

So: **an integer literal defaults to `int`; a floating literal defaults to
`double`.**

## 3. `typedef` and `enum`

```c
typedef int units;         /* units is now an alias for int */
typedef float marks;

units b1, b2;               /* declares two ints */
marks name1[50], name2[50]; /* declares two float arrays */
```

```c
enum day {Mon, Tues, Wed, Thurs, Fri, Sat, Sun};
/*          0    1    2    3     4    5    6   <- assigned by the compiler */
enum day week_st, week_end;
week_st = Mon;
```

An enumerator's value defaults to `0` for the first name and increments by 1
for each following name, unless the code assigns values explicitly.

## 4. Storage class and scope

```c
int m;                 /* global variable: seen and used anywhere in the file */

main()
{
    int i; float blc;  /* local variables: only visible inside this function */
    ...
}

function1()
{
    int i;              /* a DIFFERENT i, local to function1 */
    float sum;
    ...
}
```

| storage class | meaning |
|---|---|
| `auto` | **default.** Local variable known only to the function where it is declared |
| `static` | Local variable that **keeps its value** between calls, after control returns to the caller |
| `extern` | Global variable, known to every function in the file |
| `register` | Local variable the programmer asks the compiler to keep in a CPU register |

- `static` and `extern` variables are **automatically initialized to zero** if
  no explicit initializer is given.
- `auto` (plain local) variables are **not** initialized — they hold garbage.

## 5. Assigning and initializing values

```c
initial_value = 0;
final_value = 100;
balance = 75.84;
yes = 'x';

initial_value = 0; final_value = 100;   /* several statements, one line */
p = q = s = 0;                          /* chained assignment: right to left */
```

**Declaration + initialization** combines the two:

```c
int final_value = 100;
char yes = 'x';
```

## 6. Reading input with `scanf`

```c
int age;
printf("Enter your age: \n");
scanf("%d", &age);
```

- `scanf`'s format string should hold **only conversion specs**, never a
  prompt — print the prompt with `printf` first.
- The `&` before `age` passes the variable's **address**, so `scanf` can write
  the value back into it.

## 7. Symbolic constants: `#define`

```c
#define PI 3.14159
#define MAX 200
```

| statement | validity | why |
|---|---|---|
| `#define X = 2.5` | invalid | `=` is not allowed |
| `# define MAX 10` | invalid | no whitespace between `#` and `define` |
| `#define N 25;` | invalid | **no semicolon** at the end |
| `#define N 5, M 10` | invalid | one name per `#define` statement |
| `#define PRICE$ 100` | invalid | `$` is not permitted in the name |

A `#define`d constant **cannot be reassigned** later: `MAX = 120;` is illegal.

## 8. `const` and `volatile`

```c
const int class_size = 40;    /* cannot be changed after initialization */
volatile int date;            /* may change at any time from outside the program */
```

## 9. Common programming errors

| kind | detected | symptom |
|---|---|---|
| **Syntax error** | during compilation (translation) | the program does not compile / run at all |
| **Run-time error** | during execution | an illegal operation (e.g. divide by zero) stops the program with a diagnostic message |
| **Logic / design error** | not detected automatically | no error message — only wrong output; found by comparing results, prevented by checking the algorithm before typing code |

---

## To remember

- Integer literal → `int` by default; floating literal → `double` by default.
  Suffixes `U`/`L`/`UL`/`f` change that.
- `auto` (default, local, not initialized) vs `static` (local, keeps its
  value, zero-initialized) vs `extern` (global) vs `register` (hint for a
  CPU register).
- `#define` is text substitution: no `=`, no `;`, one name per line, name
  cannot contain `$`.
- `const` forbids reassignment; `volatile` tells the compiler the value can
  change outside the program's control.
- Syntax error (compile-time) → run-time error (execution, e.g. div by 0) →
  logic error (wrong output, no message at all).

questions.question_text: Which two families make up C's integral data types?
questions.choice_a: Integer and character
questions.choice_b: Integer and floating point
questions.choice_c: Character and void
questions.choice_d: Signed and array
questions.explanation: The integral type splits into integer (int, short int, long int, each signed or unsigned) and character (char, signed char, unsigned char).

questions.question_text: On a 32-bit machine, what is the range of a plain `int`?
questions.explanation: On the widely-used 32-bit machine, int is 32 bits: -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647.

questions.question_text: On a 16-bit machine, how many bits does a plain `int` occupy?
questions.explanation: On a 16-bit machine int is 16 bits (-32,768 to 32,767); it grows to 32 bits on the more common 32-bit machine.

questions.question_text: What is the size and range of `char`?
questions.choice_b: 8 bits, -128 to 127
questions.choice_c: 8 bits, 0 to 127
questions.explanation: char is 8 bits on both 16-bit and 32-bit machines, signed range -128 to 127 (unsigned char: 0 to 255).

questions.question_text: Which floating-point type has 64 bits and about 14 digits of precision?
questions.choice_a: float
questions.choice_b: double
questions.choice_c: long double
questions.choice_d: unsigned
questions.explanation: float is 32 bits / 6 digits of precision; double is 64 bits / 14 digits; long double is 80 bits.

questions.question_text: By default, what type does the integer literal `+111` have?
questions.choice_a: unsigned int
questions.choice_b: long int
questions.choice_c: int
questions.choice_d: double
questions.explanation: An integer constant with no suffix defaults to int, regardless of sign.

questions.question_text: By default, what type does the floating literal `12.0` have?
questions.choice_a: float
questions.choice_b: double
questions.choice_c: long double
questions.choice_d: int
questions.explanation: A floating-point constant with no suffix defaults to double.

questions.question_text: What does the `U` suffix do to an integer literal, as in `45678U`?
questions.choice_a: Marks it as unsigned int
questions.choice_b: Marks it as a float
questions.choice_c: Marks it as a character literal
questions.choice_d: Has no effect, it is decorative
questions.explanation: The U suffix makes 45678U an unsigned int constant instead of the default int.

questions.question_text: What type does `-1.2f` have?
questions.choice_a: double
questions.choice_b: long double
questions.choice_c: float
questions.choice_d: int
questions.explanation: The f suffix forces a floating literal to be float instead of the default double.

questions.question_text: Given `typedef int units;` followed by `units b1, b2;`, what are `b1` and `b2`?
questions.choice_a: Two variables of a new type unrelated to int
questions.choice_b: Two int variables, `units` being just an alias for int
questions.choice_c: A compile error, typedef cannot alias int
questions.choice_d: Two function prototypes
questions.explanation: typedef only introduces an alias name for an existing type; units b1, b2 declares two ordinary int variables.

questions.question_text: In `enum day {Mon, Tues, Wed, Thurs, Fri, Sat, Sun};`, what value does the compiler assign to `Mon` by default?
questions.choice_d: It is left undefined
questions.explanation: Enumerator values are assigned by the compiler starting at 0 for the first name and incrementing by 1, unless the code overrides them.

questions.question_text: Where is a global variable declared, and where is it visible?
questions.choice_a: Inside main() only; visible only in main()
questions.choice_b: Outside every function; visible to every function in the file
questions.choice_c: Inside each function separately; a copy per function
questions.choice_d: Only inside the function that uses it first
questions.explanation: A global variable is declared outside all functions and can be seen and used anywhere in the file, unlike local variables restricted to their own function.

questions.question_text: Which storage class is the default for a variable declared inside a function with no explicit specifier?
questions.choice_a: static
questions.choice_b: extern
questions.choice_c: register
questions.choice_d: auto
questions.explanation: auto is the default storage class: a local variable known only to the function in which it is declared.

questions.question_text: Which storage class specifier makes a local variable keep its value between successive calls to its function?
questions.choice_a: auto
questions.choice_b: static
questions.choice_c: register
questions.choice_d: extern
questions.explanation: static gives a local variable a lifetime that spans the whole program run: it retains its value even after control returns to the caller.

questions.question_text: What does the `register` storage class specifier ask the compiler to do?
questions.choice_a: Zero-initialize the variable automatically
questions.choice_b: Make the variable visible to every function in the file
questions.choice_c: Store the local variable in a CPU register for faster access
questions.choice_d: Forbid the variable from ever changing
questions.explanation: register is a hint that the variable should be kept in a register rather than ordinary memory, for speed.

questions.question_text: If no initializer is given, what value do `static` and `extern` variables start with?
questions.choice_a: Zero, automatically
questions.choice_b: Garbage, like auto variables
questions.choice_c: The value 1
questions.choice_d: It is a compile error to leave them uninitialized
questions.explanation: static and extern variables are automatically initialized to zero; auto (plain local) variables are not initialized and contain garbage.

questions.question_text: Why is `#define N 25;` invalid?
questions.choice_a: N is not a valid identifier
questions.choice_b: 25 must be written as 25.0
questions.choice_c: A #define statement must not end with a semicolon
questions.choice_d: #define cannot be used for numbers
questions.explanation: Unlike a C statement, #define takes no trailing semicolon; a ';' would become part of the substituted text.

questions.question_text: After `#define MAX 200`, what happens with `MAX = 120;` later in the code?
questions.choice_a: MAX is updated to 120
questions.choice_b: It is illegal: a #define'd constant cannot be reassigned
questions.choice_c: It silently does nothing
questions.choice_d: It redefines the macro for the rest of the file
questions.explanation: #define performs pure text substitution before compilation; the resulting code (200 = 120;) is not a valid assignment, so it is illegal.

questions.question_text: What does declaring `const int class_size = 40;` guarantee?
questions.choice_a: class_size can only be changed by other files
questions.choice_b: class_size cannot be changed after its initialization
questions.choice_c: class_size is automatically zero if unused
questions.choice_d: class_size is stored in a register
questions.explanation: const marks the variable as read-only after initialization: any later assignment to it is illegal.

questions.question_text: What does the `volatile` qualifier tell the compiler about a variable, as in `volatile int date;`?
questions.choice_a: The variable must never change
questions.choice_b: The variable's value may change at any time from outside the program's own control flow
questions.choice_c: The variable is always zero-initialized
questions.choice_d: The variable must be stored in a CPU register
questions.explanation: volatile warns the compiler that the value can be altered externally (hardware, another thread), so it must not be cached or optimized away between reads.

questions.question_text: In `scanf("%d", &age);`, what is the purpose of the `&` before `age`?
questions.choice_a: It converts age to a string
questions.choice_b: It passes the address of age so scanf can write the value into it
questions.choice_c: It is optional, only used for style
questions.choice_d: It forces age to be unsigned
questions.explanation: C passes arguments by value; & passes age's address instead, letting scanf store the read value directly into the variable.

questions.question_text: Which kind of programming error is detected during compilation, before the program can even run?
questions.choice_a: Logic error
questions.choice_b: Run-time error
questions.choice_c: Syntax error
questions.choice_d: Design error
questions.explanation: A syntax error violates the C grammar rules and is caught during translation (compilation); the program cannot be executed until it is fixed.

questions.question_text: Dividing a number by zero at execution time is an example of which kind of error?
questions.choice_a: Syntax error
questions.choice_b: Run-time error
questions.choice_c: Logic error
questions.choice_d: None, it always compiles and runs fine
questions.explanation: A run-time error is an attempt at an invalid operation detected during execution; the computer stops and displays a diagnostic message.

questions.question_text: A program compiles, runs to completion, and prints no error message, but the result is wrong. What kind of error is this?
questions.choice_a: Syntax error
questions.choice_b: Run-time error
questions.choice_c: Logic (design) error
questions.choice_d: It cannot be a bug if there is no error message
questions.explanation: A logic error follows an incorrect algorithm: no syntax or run-time error is raised, only incorrect output, found by comparing results to what is expected.

exercises.prompt: What is the default storage class of a variable declared inside a function, with no explicit specifier written?
exercises.explanation: auto is the default: local, known only within the function, not automatically initialized.

exercises.prompt: Which storage class specifier keeps a local variable's value alive between successive calls to its function?
exercises.explanation: static gives the variable a lifetime spanning the whole program run, unlike the default auto which resets each call.

exercises.prompt: An integer literal like `45678` with no suffix defaults to which C type?
exercises.explanation: Integer constants default to int unless a U, L, or UL suffix says otherwise.

exercises.prompt: A floating-point literal like `1.234` with no suffix defaults to which C type?
exercises.explanation: Floating constants default to double; the f suffix is needed to force float instead.

exercises.prompt: Order the three kinds of programming errors by when each one is typically detected.
steps: Syntax error — caught while the compiler translates the source code, before it can run
Run-time error — caught while the program executes, e.g. a division by zero stops it with a diagnostic
Logic (design) error — never raises a message; only found afterwards by comparing the program's output to the expected result
exercises.explanation: Compilation catches syntax errors first; execution can then surface run-time errors; a logic error produces no error at all, only wrong output, and is caught only by checking results.

exercises.prompt: Order these by scope and lifetime, from most local and short-lived to most global.
steps: auto (default) — local to the function, exists only while that function call is active
static — local to the function, but keeps its value across calls for the whole program run
extern — global, declared outside every function, visible to and shared by every function in the file
exercises.explanation: auto is confined to one call; static survives across calls but stays private to its function; extern is visible file-wide.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart of the investment program (Fig. 2.10): read amount, interest rate and period, then print the value at the end of each year while year <= period.
exercises.hint: Linear read/init, then a loop: while year <= period, compute value, display it, update amount and year; when the loop ends, stop. One decision node.
exercises.explanation: The while loop tests year <= period before each pass: compute this year's value, display it, reinvest (amount = value) and advance year, then loop back to the test.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart of Fig. 2.12: print a Fahrenheit-to-Celsius table from F_LOW to F_MAX in steps of STEP.
exercises.hint: Init fahrenheit = F_LOW, then loop while fahrenheit <= F_MAX: compute celsius, display both, add STEP to fahrenheit. One decision node.
exercises.explanation: F_LOW, F_MAX and STEP are symbolic constants (#define). The loop tests fahrenheit <= F_MAX, prints one converted line per pass, then advances by STEP before testing again.

exercises.prompt: Which of these #define statements is invalid, and why? `#define PRICE$ 100`
choices: Invalid: the $ symbol is not permitted in a macro name
Valid: PRICE$ is a perfectly normal identifier
Invalid: PRICE must be written in lowercase
exercises.explanation: The $ symbol is not permitted in a #define name; PRICE_100 or similar would be valid.

exercises.prompt: Which of these #define statements is invalid, and why? `#define N 5, M 10`
choices: Invalid: a single #define statement can only define one name
Invalid: numbers cannot be separated by commas anywhere in C
Valid: it defines both N and M at once
Invalid: N and M must start with a lowercase letter
exercises.explanation: Each #define statement defines exactly one symbolic name; N and M need two separate #define lines.

lesson:
# Database Design — Week 3

Lecture 05 — *E-R Diagrams – 2*. Roles, recursive relationship sets, mapping
cardinality, participation constraints, weak entity sets, superclass /
subclass, generalization vs specialization, and a full worked example (the NHL
database).

---

## 0. The symbols, all in one place

```er
{
  "title": "E-R diagram symbols (Chen notation, as used in the course).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "e", "kind": "entity", "label": "Strong entity set", "x": 130, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "w", "kind": "weak_entity", "label": "Weak entity set", "x": 130, "y": 115 },
    { "id": "r", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Strong relationship", "x": 130, "y": 205 },
    { "id": "ir", "kind": "identifying_relationship", "label": "Weak relationship", "x": 130, "y": 300 },
    { "id": "isa", "kind": "isa", "label": "ISA", "x": 130, "y": 385 },
    { "id": "a", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Simple attribute", "x": 450, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "k", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "Key attribute", "x": 450, "y": 105 },
    { "id": "pk", "kind": "partial_key_attribute", "label": "Partial key (discriminator)", "x": 450, "y": 170 },
    { "id": "m", "kind": "multi_attribute", "label": "Multivalued attribute", "x": 450, "y": 240 },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "derived_attribute", "label": "Derived attribute", "x": 450, "y": 310 },
    { "id": "c", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Composite attribute", "x": 450, "y": 375 },
    { "id": "c1", "kind": "attribute", "label": "part 1", "x": 380, "y": 440 },
    { "id": "c2", "kind": "attribute", "label": "part 2", "x": 520, "y": 440 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "c", "to": "c1" }, { "from": "c", "to": "c2" }
  ]
}
```

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| rectangle | strong entity set (has its own primary key) |
| **double** rectangle | **weak** entity set (no primary key of its own) |
| diamond | relationship set |
| **double** diamond | **identifying** (weak) relationship, tying a weak entity to its strong entity |
| oval | attribute; **underlined** = key attribute; **dashed underline** = discriminator; **double** oval = multivalued; **dashed** oval = derived; oval with sub-ovals = composite |
| triangle "ISA" | superclass / subclass link (generalization, specialization) |
| single line | (partial) participation of an entity set in a relationship |
| **double** line | **total** participation |
| `1` / `N` on a line | mapping cardinality |

## 1. Role names

**Roles** are indicated by **labelling the lines** that connect a diamond
(relationship) to a rectangle (entity). Role labels are **optional**; they are
used to clarify the **semantics** (meaning) of the relationship — especially
when the same entity set appears twice.

```er
{
  "title": "Faculty takes part in Reports_To twice, once as Coordinator and once as Head: the two labels are roles.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "f", "kind": "entity", "label": "Faculty", "x": 200, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "id", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "EmpID", "x": 100, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "nm", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Name", "x": 270, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "br", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Branch", "x": 100, "y": 270 },
    { "id": "ex", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Experience", "x": 280, "y": 280 },
    { "id": "r", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Reports_To", "x": 520, "y": 160 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "f", "to": "id" }, { "from": "f", "to": "nm" }, { "from": "f", "to": "br" }, { "from": "f", "to": "ex" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "r", "role": "Coordinator" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "r", "role": "Head" }
  ]
}
```

The labels *Coordinator* and *Head* specify **which Faculty entities interact
with which** via the `Reports_To` relationship set.

## 2. Recursive relationship set

When **the same entity set participates in a relationship set more than
once**, the relationship set is **recursive**. `Reports_To` above is recursive:
both of its ends are `Faculty`.

```er
{
  "title": "Faculty works in a Department (ordinary binary relationship) and Faculty reports to Faculty (recursive relationship set).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "f", "kind": "entity", "label": "Faculty", "x": 160, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "fi", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "FacID", "x": 60, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "fn", "kind": "attribute", "label": "FName", "x": 220, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "po", "kind": "attribute", "label": "Post", "x": 40, "y": 260 },
    { "id": "w", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Works", "x": 380, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "d", "kind": "entity", "label": "Department", "x": 590, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "di", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "DeptID", "x": 520, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "dn", "kind": "attribute", "label": "DName", "x": 660, "y": 60 },
    { "id": "rr", "kind": "relationship", "label": "Reports_To", "x": 160, "y": 330 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "f", "to": "fi" }, { "from": "f", "to": "fn" }, { "from": "f", "to": "po" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "w" }, { "from": "w", "to": "d" },
    { "from": "d", "to": "di" }, { "from": "d", "to": "dn" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "rr", "role": "HOD" },
    { "from": "f", "to": "rr", "role": "Prof." }
  ]
}
```

With data, the recursion is obvious: a professor's *head* is another row of the
same `Faculty` table.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Instances: Lee and Kim (professors) report to David (HOD) — all three are Faculty rows.",
```

## 3. Mapping cardinality (cardinality constraints)

The mapping cardinality represents **the number of entities of another entity
set that can be connected to one entity through a relationship set**. It is
most useful for describing **binary** relationship sets, where it must be one
of four types. The examples use `customer` —`borrow`— `loan`.

## 4. Participation constraints

A participation constraint specifies **the participation of an entity set in a
relationship set**. Two kinds:

| Kind | Meaning | Drawn as |
|---|---|---|
| **Partial participation** | **some** entities of the set may **not participate** in any relationship of the set | **single line** |
| **Total participation** | **every** entity of the set participates in **at least one** relationship of the set | **double line** |

## 5. Weak entity sets

An entity set that **does not have a primary key** is called a **weak entity
set**. Its existence **depends on the existence of a strong entity set**.

```er
{
  "title": "loan (strong entity set) — L_P (weak / identifying relationship, double diamond) — payment (weak entity set, double rectangle). payment-no is the discriminator (dashed underline).",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "l", "kind": "entity", "label": "loan", "x": 150, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "ln", "kind": "key_attribute", "label": "loan-no", "x": 70, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "am", "kind": "attribute", "label": "amount", "x": 210, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "lp", "kind": "identifying_relationship", "label": "L_P", "x": 350, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "p", "kind": "weak_entity", "label": "payment", "x": 560, "y": 160 },
    { "id": "pn", "kind": "partial_key_attribute", "label": "payment-no", "x": 450, "y": 50 },
    { "id": "pd", "kind": "attribute", "label": "payment-date", "x": 600, "y": 40 },
    { "id": "pa", "kind": "attribute", "label": "payment-amount", "x": 620, "y": 270 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "l", "to": "ln" }, { "from": "l", "to": "am" },
    { "from": "l", "to": "lp", "card": "1" },
    { "from": "lp", "to": "p", "card": "N", "total": true },
    { "from": "p", "to": "pn" }, { "from": "p", "to": "pd" }, { "from": "p", "to": "pa" }
  ]
}
```

- Drawn as a **double rectangle**; the relationship that ties it to its strong
  entity (the **weak entity relationship**, or identifying relationship) is a
  **double diamond**.
- The **discriminator** (**partial key**) of a weak entity set is the set of
  attributes that distinguishes all the entities of the weak entity set *among
  those attached to the same strong entity*. It is underlined with a **dashed
  line**.
- The **primary key** of a weak entity set = **primary key of the strong entity
  set** it depends on **+ its own discriminator**.
- Example: `payment` has `payment-no` as discriminator; `loan` has `loan-no` as
  primary key; so the primary key of `payment` is **(loan-no, payment-no)**.
  Payment n° 1 of loan 17 and payment n° 1 of loan 42 are two different
  payments — `payment-no` alone cannot tell them apart.
- A weak entity always participates **totally** in its identifying relationship
  (a payment cannot exist without its loan), hence the double line on the
  `payment` side.

## 6. Superclass vs subclass

| Super class | Sub class |
|---|---|
| an entity from which **other entities can be derived** | an entity that is **derived from another entity** |
| `Account` has two subsets, `Saving_Account` and `Current_Account`, so `Account` is a superclass | `Saving_Account` and `Current_Account` are derived from `Account`, so they are subclasses |
