A subclass **inherits** all the attributes of its superclass and adds its own.

## 7. Generalization vs specialization

Both produce the **same picture** — a superclass above an ISA triangle,
subclasses below — but they are built in **opposite directions**.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Generalization builds the superclass bottom-up from common features; specialization splits a superclass top-down into subsets.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "h1", "x": 160, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "Generalization — bottom-up", "bold": true },
    { "id": "h2", "x": 500, "y": 12, "shape": "text", "label": "Specialization — top-down", "bold": true },
    { "id": "g1", "x": 160, "y": 60, "w": 200, "h": 40, "label": "Person\n(Name, Address)", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true },
    { "id": "g2", "x": 80, "y": 200, "w": 130, "h": 40, "label": "Student\n(Name, Address, SPI)", "tone": "sky", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "g3", "x": 240, "y": 200, "w": 140, "h": 40, "label": "Faculty\n(Name, Address, Salary)", "tone": "sky", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "gn", "x": 160, "y": 245, "shape": "text", "label": "↑ extract the common features", "size": 11 },
    { "id": "s1", "x": 500, "y": 60, "w": 200, "h": 40, "label": "Person\n(Name, Address)", "tone": "sky" },
    { "id": "s2", "x": 420, "y": 200, "w": 130, "h": 40, "label": "Student\n(+ SPI)", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "s3", "x": 580, "y": 200, "w": 130, "h": 40, "label": "Faculty\n(+ Salary)", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "sn", "x": 500, "y": 245, "shape": "text", "label": "↓ split by distinguishing features", "size": 11 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "g2", "to": "g1", "tone": "emerald" }, { "from": "g3", "to": "g1", "tone": "emerald" },
    { "from": "s1", "to": "s2", "tone": "emerald" }, { "from": "s1", "to": "s3", "tone": "emerald" }
  ]
}
```

| | Generalization | Specialization |
|---|---|---|
| definition | **extracts the common features of multiple entities to form a new entity** | **splits an entity to form multiple new entities that inherit some feature of the splitting entity** |
| process | creation of a **group** from various entities | creation of **sub-groups** within an entity |
| approach | **bottom-up** | **top-down** |
| set operation | takes the **union** of two or more **lower-level** entity sets to produce a **higher-level** entity set | takes a **subset** of a **higher-level** entity set to form a **lower-level** entity set |
| starting point | starts from **several** entity sets and creates a high-level entity set using their **common** features | starts from a **single** entity set and creates different low-level entity sets using **different** features |

Example from the slides: `Student(Name, Address, SPI)` and `Faculty(Name,
Address, Salary)` share `Name` and `Address` → generalize into `Person(Name,
Address)`; conversely, `Person` specializes into `Student` (adds `SPI`) and
`Faculty` (adds `Salary`).

## 8. Worked example — the NHL database

> The NHL has many **teams**; each team has a name, a city, a coach, a captain
> and a set of players. Each **player** belongs to only one team; a player has a
> name, a position (left wing, goalie…), a skill level and a set of **injury
> records**. A team captain is also a player. A **game** is played between two
> teams (host team and guest team) and has a date and a score. Construct a
> clean and concise E-R diagram.

Method — the same five steps for any description:

1. **Entities** (nouns that have their own data): team, player, game, injury
   record → rectangles.
2. **Attributes** for each, and the **primary key** underlined. An injury
   record has no key of its own — it only makes sense for a given player →
   **weak entity** with a discriminator.
3. **Relationships** (verbs): a player *belongs to* a team; a team *has a
   captain*; a game is *hosted by* a team and *visited by* a team; a player
   *logs* injury records.
4. **Roles** where one entity plays two parts in one relationship (a team is
   `host` in one game and `guest` in another).
5. **Cardinality and participation** on every line.


Reading the answer:

- `belongs_to` is **1 : N** (one team, many players) with **total**
  participation of `player` — every player belongs to a team.
- `captain` is **1 : 1** — one captain per team, and that captain is a player
  (so no separate *captain* entity: the relationship does the job).
- `host` and `guest` are two relationships between `game` and `team`; each
  game has exactly **one** host and **one** guest (total on the game side), a
  team can host or visit **many** games.
- `injury record` is **weak**: identified by `(p-name, id)` through the
  identifying relationship `log` (double diamond, double line).

---

## To remember

- **Role** = label on a line, needed when the same entity set takes part twice
  in one relationship (**recursive** relationship set).
- **Mapping cardinality** of a binary relationship: **1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:N** —
  the `1`/`N` on one side says how many of *that* side one entity of the other
  side can have.
- **Participation**: single line = **partial** (some entities may not take
  part), double line = **total** (every entity takes part).
- **Weak entity set** = no primary key of its own; **double rectangle**, tied
  by a **double diamond** (identifying relationship); **discriminator** with a
  **dashed underline**; primary key = strong key + discriminator.
- **Superclass / subclass** linked through the **ISA** triangle; the subclass
  inherits the superclass's attributes.
- **Generalization = bottom-up** (union of lower-level sets into one
  higher-level set, from common features); **specialization = top-down**
  (subsets of a higher-level set, from distinguishing features).
- Method for any statement: entities → attributes & keys → relationships →
  roles → cardinality & participation.

questions.question_text: What is a role, in an E-R diagram?
questions.choice_a: The primary key of an entity
questions.choice_b: A label on the line connecting a relationship to an entity, clarifying how that entity participates
questions.choice_c: A synonym for the relationship's name
questions.choice_d: The cardinality written on a line
questions.explanation: Roles are indicated by labeling the lines that connect diamonds (relationship) to rectangles (entity); they clarify semantics and are optional.

questions.question_text: In the Faculty — Reports_To example, 'Coordinator' and 'Head' are examples of what?
questions.choice_a: Two different entity sets
questions.choice_b: Role names on the same recursive relationship
questions.choice_c: Two separate primary keys
questions.choice_d: Weak entity discriminators
questions.explanation: Coordinator and Head are role labels: they specify which Faculty entities interact with whom via the Reports_To relationship set.

questions.question_text: What makes a relationship set 'recursive'?
questions.choice_a: It has more than one attribute
questions.choice_b: The same entity set participates in the relationship set more than once
questions.choice_c: It connects three or more different entity sets
questions.choice_d: It has no cardinality constraint
questions.explanation: A recursive relationship set is one where the same entity participates in the relationship more than once, e.g. Faculty reporting to another Faculty.

questions.question_text: What does mapping cardinality describe?
questions.choice_a: The number of attributes an entity has
questions.choice_b: The number of entities of another set connected to an entity via a relationship set
questions.choice_c: Whether an entity set is weak or strong
questions.choice_d: The physical storage size of a table
questions.explanation: Mapping cardinality is most useful for describing binary relationship sets, and comes in four types: 1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:N.

questions.question_text: A customer holds exactly one loan, and that loan belongs to exactly one customer. What mapping cardinality is this?
questions.choice_a: One-to-many
questions.choice_b: Many-to-one
questions.choice_c: One-to-one
questions.choice_d: Many-to-many
questions.explanation: Both sides are restricted to exactly one: an entity in A is associated with only one entity in B and vice versa, which is 1:1.

questions.question_text: A loan is connected with more than one customer, and a customer is connected with only one loan. What mapping cardinality is this (from loan's perspective toward customer)?
questions.choice_a: One-to-one
questions.choice_b: Many-to-one
questions.choice_c: Many-to-many
questions.choice_d: One-to-many
questions.explanation: An entity in A (loan) is associated with more than one entity in B (customer), and each B is associated with only one A: that is one-to-many for loan-to-customer.

questions.question_text: In a many-to-many (N-N) relationship between customer and loan, what holds?
questions.choice_a: A customer can have only one loan and a loan only one customer
questions.choice_b: A customer can be connected with more than one loan, and a loan can be connected with more than one customer
questions.choice_c: Only customers can have multiple connections, loans cannot
questions.choice_d: N-N relationships are not allowed between binary entity sets
questions.explanation: Many-to-many means both sides can connect to more than one entity of the other set.

questions.question_text: What do participation constraints specify?
questions.choice_a: The maximum number of attributes an entity can have
questions.choice_b: The participation of an entity set in a relationship set: whether every entity must take part
questions.choice_c: The order in which relationships are drawn
questions.choice_d: Which entity set is the primary key holder
questions.explanation: Participation constraints describe whether every entity in a set participates in at least one relationship (total) or not (partial).

questions.question_text: How is total participation represented on an E-R diagram?
questions.choice_a: A dashed line
questions.choice_b: A single line
questions.choice_c: A double line
questions.choice_d: An arrow
questions.explanation: Total participation, where every entity in the set participates in at least one relationship, is drawn with a double line.

questions.question_text: How is partial participation represented on an E-R diagram?
questions.choice_a: A double line
questions.choice_b: A single line
questions.choice_c: A dotted oval
questions.choice_d: A double diamond
questions.explanation: Partial participation, where some entities may not participate in any relationship, is drawn with a single line.

questions.question_text: What is a weak entity set?
questions.choice_a: An entity set with fewer than three attributes
questions.choice_b: An entity set that does not have a primary key of its own
questions.choice_c: An entity set that only appears in recursive relationships
questions.choice_d: An entity set with no relationships at all
questions.explanation: A weak entity set is defined as an entity set that does not have a primary key; its identity depends on a strong entity set.

questions.question_text: What is a weak entity set's discriminator?
questions.choice_a: Its full primary key
questions.choice_b: The set of attributes that distinguishes all the entities of the weak entity set
questions.choice_c: A foreign key pointing at the strong entity
questions.choice_d: The relationship diamond connecting it to the strong entity
questions.explanation: The discriminator (partial key) is the attribute set that distinguishes the weak entity's own entities; it is not, by itself, a full primary key.

questions.question_text: How do you form the actual primary key of a weak entity set?
questions.choice_a: Use the discriminator alone
questions.choice_b: Combine the primary key of the identifying strong entity set with the weak entity's discriminator
questions.choice_c: Use the relationship's name as the key
questions.choice_d: Weak entity sets never have a usable primary key
questions.explanation: The primary key of a weak entity set is created by combining the identifying strong entity set's primary key with the weak entity's own discriminator, e.g. (loan-no, payment-no).

questions.question_text: How is the discriminator attribute of a weak entity set underlined?
questions.choice_a: With a solid line, exactly like an ordinary primary key
questions.choice_b: With a dashed line
questions.choice_c: It is never underlined
questions.choice_d: With a double line
questions.explanation: The discriminator (partial key) is underlined with a dashed line, distinguishing it visually from a full, solid-underlined primary key.

questions.question_text: How is a weak entity set itself drawn on the diagram?
questions.choice_a: As a diamond
questions.choice_b: As a single rectangle
questions.choice_c: As a double rectangle
questions.choice_d: As a dashed oval
questions.explanation: A weak entity set is indicated by a double rectangle; the identifying relationship that ties it to its strong entity is a double diamond.

questions.question_text: If `account` is an entity with two subsets `saving_account` and `current_account`, which is the superclass?
questions.choice_a: saving_account
questions.choice_b: current_account
questions.choice_c: account
questions.choice_d: None of them, superclasses do not apply here
questions.explanation: account is the superclass: another entity (saving_account, current_account) can be derived from it. Those two are the subclasses.

questions.question_text: What is the process of extracting the common features of multiple entities to form one new, higher-level entity called?
questions.choice_a: Specialization
questions.choice_b: Generalization
questions.choice_c: Normalization
questions.choice_d: Weak entity resolution
questions.explanation: Generalization extracts the common features of multiple entities to form a new (higher-level) entity, using a bottom-up approach.

questions.question_text: What is the process of splitting one entity into multiple new entities that each inherit some of its features called?
questions.choice_a: Generalization
questions.choice_b: Specialization
questions.choice_c: Weak entity discrimination
questions.choice_d: Recursive relationship resolution
questions.explanation: Specialization splits an entity to form new entities that inherit some of its features, using a top-down approach.

questions.question_text: Generalization takes the union of two or more lower-level entity sets to produce a higher-level entity set. What approach is this?
questions.choice_a: Top-down
questions.choice_b: Bottom-up
questions.choice_c: Left-to-right
questions.choice_d: Depth-first
questions.explanation: Generalization starts from a number of entity sets and builds a high-level entity set using common features: a bottom-up approach.

questions.question_text: Specialization takes a subset of a higher-level entity set to form a lower-level entity set. What approach is this?
questions.choice_a: Bottom-up
questions.choice_b: Top-down
questions.choice_c: Breadth-first
questions.choice_d: Recursive
questions.explanation: Specialization starts from a single entity set and creates different low-level entity sets using distinguishing features: a top-down approach.

questions.question_text: In an ISA hierarchy such as Person — ISA — {Student, Faculty}, what does the ISA triangle represent?
questions.choice_a: A weak entity relationship
questions.choice_b: A generalization/specialization link between a superclass and its subclasses
questions.choice_c: A cardinality constraint of many-to-many
questions.choice_d: A recursive relationship set
questions.explanation: The ISA triangle is the notation for a generalization/specialization hierarchy: Student and Faculty are subclasses derived from the Person superclass.

exercises.prompt: In an E-R diagram, what kind of participation is drawn with a double line between an entity and a relationship diamond?
exercises.explanation: Total participation (every entity of the set must appear in the relationship) is drawn with a double line; partial participation uses a single line.

exercises.prompt: What kind of entity set has no primary key of its own and depends on a strong entity set for its identity?
exercises.explanation: A weak entity set has no primary key; its real primary key combines its own discriminator with the identifying strong entity set's key.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to build an E-R diagram from a written description (e.g. the NHL database).
steps: Identify the entities and draw a rectangle for each
Attach each entity's attributes as ovals and underline the primary key
Identify the relationships between entities and draw a diamond for each
Add role names on the lines where an entity plays more than one part (recursive or ambiguous relationships)
Label each relationship's cardinality (1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:N)
Mark each relationship's participation constraints (single line = partial, double line = total)
exercises.explanation: Entities and their attributes come first, then the relationships between them, then the refinements — roles, cardinality, participation — that make the diagram precise.

exercises.prompt: Order the four mapping cardinalities from the most restrictive to the least restrictive (fewest possible connections to most).
steps: One-to-one (1:1) — each side connects to at most one entity of the other
One-to-many (1:N) or many-to-one (N:1) — one side connects to many, the other to only one
Many-to-many (N:N) — both sides can connect to many entities of the other set
exercises.explanation: 1:1 is the tightest constraint (one on both sides), N:N the loosest (many on both sides); 1:N/N:1 sit in between, restricting exactly one side.

exercises.prompt: Draw the customer–loan relationship 'borrow' as a many-to-many (N:N) relationship, with total participation on the loan side (every loan must have a customer) and partial participation on the customer side.
exercises.hint: Two entities (customer, loan) and a relationship diamond (borrow) between them. Click the loan–borrow line twice to cycle its cardinality to N, and the customer–borrow line to N as well.
exercises.explanation: A customer may hold several loans and a loan may be shared by several customers, so both sides of borrow carry an N cardinality: many-to-many.

exercises.prompt: Draw the weak entity set 'payment', identified through the strong entity 'loan' by the weak (double) relationship 'L_P', each with one key attribute.
exercises.hint: loan is a plain (single) rectangle with its key attribute loan-no. payment is a weak entity (double rectangle) with its discriminator payment-no (use the “Discriminator (partial key)” shape: dashed underline), joined to loan through the weak relationship L_P (double diamond).
exercises.explanation: loan is strong (single rectangle, own primary key loan-no); payment has no primary key of its own so it is weak (double rectangle), tied to loan through the identifying (double-diamond) relationship L_P. Its real primary key is (loan-no, payment-no).

exercises.prompt: Draw the generalization/specialization hierarchy: Person is the superclass; Student and Faculty are its subclasses (one ISA link).
exercises.hint: One entity Person, an ISA node, and two entities Student and Faculty below it. The ISA node sits between Person (above) and the two subclasses (below).
exercises.explanation: The ISA triangle links the superclass Person to its subclasses Student and Faculty, each inheriting Person's shared attributes while adding their own.

exercises.prompt: Which pair correctly matches the total/partial participation marks used in an E-R diagram?
choices: Total = double line, Partial = single line
Total = single line, Partial = double line
Total = dashed line, Partial = solid line
Total and Partial use the same mark; only the cardinality label differs
exercises.explanation: Total participation (every entity of the set is involved) is drawn with a double line; partial participation is a single line.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: 1 on the customer side, N on the loan side: one customer may hold many loans, each loan belongs to one customer.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: N on the customer side, 1 on the loan side: several customers can share one loan (a joint loan), each customer holds a single loan.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: N on both sides: many customers, many loans.

exercises.prompt: What is the mapping cardinality of this relationship?
exercises.explanation: 1 on both sides.

exercises.prompt: What does the double line on the loan side mean?
choices: Total participation: every loan takes part in borrow
Partial participation: some loans have no customer
exercises.explanation: A double line is total participation — every entity of the set participates in at least one relationship. Cardinality is the 1/N mark, and a weak entity would be a double rectangle.

exercises.prompt: What does the single line on the customer side mean?
choices: Partial participation: a customer may have no loan
Total participation: every customer has a loan
exercises.explanation: A single line is partial participation: some customers may not take part in any borrow relationship.

exercises.prompt: What is the primary key of the entity set payment?
exercises.explanation: payment is weak (double rectangle): payment-no is only a discriminator (dashed underline). Its primary key combines the strong entity's key with the discriminator.

exercises.prompt: What kind of entity set is payment on this diagram?
exercises.explanation: Double rectangle = weak entity set, tied to loan by the double diamond (identifying relationship).

exercises.prompt: What are Coordinator and Head on this diagram?
choices: Role names on a recursive relationship
exercises.explanation: The same entity set Faculty takes part twice in Reports_To; the labels on the two lines are roles, which clarify the meaning of each participation.

exercises.explanation: Account sits above the ISA triangle: Saving_Account and Current_Account are derived from it and inherit its attributes.

name: Week 3
lesson:
# Software Engineering — Week 3

*Agile Software Engineering — Incremental development and Scrum.*

---

## 1. Product development and uncertainty

A **product vision** identifies the proposed product, its users, and the
value it should provide. Detailed features develop as the team learns more
about users, technology, and the product's environment.

Flow: `Product vision (What/Who/Why)` → `Candidate product features` → `A
small, tested product increment` → `Evaluation and new information`, which
feeds back into refining the features.

Incremental development gives users an early opportunity to evaluate working
software; their feedback can expose missing requirements and change the
order of future work.

## 2. Plan-driven vs agile development

| | Plan-driven development | Agile development |
|---|---|---|
| **Planning** | define substantial requirements and design detail before implementation | develop near-term detail and revise later work as knowledge grows |
| **Coordination** | documents support large teams, handovers, and long system lifetimes | frequent interaction supports rapid decisions and shared understanding |
| **Change** | revise affected plans and completed development work | use frequent increments to evaluate results and redirect work |

Detailed documentation can justify its cost in critical, long-lived systems.
Agile approaches reduce overhead in rapidly evolving products.

## 3. Incremental vs iterative development

- **Incremental development**: extend the product with additional usable
  functionality. Each new addition works with what the product already
  provides (`Feature A` → `A+B` → `A+B+C`).
- **Iterative development**: revisit and improve an existing result. A later
  cycle can refine requirements, change a design, or improve behaviour after
  evaluation (`Initial version` → `Evaluate` → `Revised version`).
- The two ideas can operate together: a cycle can add a feature while
  revising earlier work.

An increment adds a small amount of functionality: **select features → refine
descriptions → implement and test → integrate and test the system → deliver
and evaluate**, with feedback informing the next selection.

```diagram
{
```

```diagram
    { "id": "s3", "x": 330, "y": 60, "w": 100, "h": 44, "label": "implement\nand test", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 12 },
    { "id": "s4", "x": 460, "y": 60, "w": 100, "h": 44, "label": "integrate and\ntest the system", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 11 },

    { "from": "s5", "to": "s1", "label": "feedback", "dashed": true, "via": [[590, 120], [70, 120]] }
  ]

```

## 4. Agile values and principles

The Agile Manifesto expresses **relative priorities** — each comparison
values both sides, with greater weight on the left:

| Greater emphasis | over | Also valuable |
|---|---|---|
| Individuals and interactions | over | Processes and tools |
| Working software | over | Comprehensive documentation |
| Customer collaboration | over | Contract negotiation |
| Responding to change | over | Following a plan |

Five agile principles:

| Principle | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Involve the customer | customers/representatives help prioritize requirements and evaluate increments |
| Embrace change | adapt features as users and developers learn more |
| Develop incrementally | develop, test, evaluate small additions; use feedback in later work |
| Maintain simplicity | reduce unnecessary complexity in software and process |
| Focus on people | trust capable team members to organize their own way of working |

## 5. Extreme Programming (XP) practices

| Practice | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Incremental planning | select work for the next increment through discussion and relative priority |
| Small releases | deliver a useful subset of functionality, add capability over time |
| Test-driven development | write a test for required behaviour before coding; rerun tests after changes |
| Continuous integration | integrate completed changes frequently, check the combined system automatically |
| Refactoring | improve code structure while preserving its externally observable behaviour |

## 6. The Scrum framework

Scrum organizes complex product development around short **Sprints** and
regular inspection: `Ordered product work` → `Sprint planning and work` →
`Usable Increment` → `Inspection and adaptation`, which updates future work.

**Empiricism and the three pillars** (each supports the next):

`Transparency` (make work, results, quality visible) → `Inspection` (examine
artifacts and progress toward agreed goals) → `Adaptation` (adjust work or
process when inspection reveals a problem) → feeds back into transparency.

```diagram
{
  "title": "Empiricism: the three pillars of Scrum feed one another in a loop.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "t", "x": 110, "y": 60, "w": 150, "h": 50, "label": "Transparency\nwork and results visible", "tone": "sky", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "i", "x": 340, "y": 60, "w": 150, "h": 50, "label": "Inspection\nexamine artifacts, progress", "tone": "amber", "filled": true, "size": 11 },
    { "id": "a", "x": 570, "y": 60, "w": 150, "h": 50, "label": "Adaptation\nadjust work or process", "tone": "emerald", "filled": true, "size": 11 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "t", "to": "i" }, { "from": "i", "to": "a" },
```

**Scrum values**: Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, Courage.

## 7. Scrum Team accountabilities

A self-managing Scrum Team combines complementary skills and three
accountabilities:

| Accountability | Primary responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Product Owner | maximize product value; communicate direction; keep the Product Backlog ordered and understandable |
| Developers | create a usable Increment; plan the Sprint's work; uphold quality; adapt the plan as development progresses |
| Scrum Master | help establish Scrum and improve team effectiveness; coach the team; help remove impediments |

**Self-managing** means the team decides who does what, when, and how — the
accountabilities do not create a command hierarchy.

## 8. Artifacts and commitments

| Artifact | Content | Commitment |
|---|---|---|
| Product Backlog | ordered, evolving list of improvements | Product Goal (longer-term direction) |
| Sprint Backlog | work and delivery plan for one Sprint | Sprint Goal (one Sprint's objective) |
| Increment | integrated, usable work | Definition of Done (required product quality) |

- The **Product Backlog** can contain new features, defect corrections,
  technical improvements, and investigation of uncertain work.
- The **Product Goal** describes a future product state; near-term items are
  detailed, further ones stay broad.
- **Backlog refinement**: a broad item is discussed, clarified, and divided
  until it is detailed enough to be selected for a Sprint.
- An **Increment** adds verified, usable work; a Sprint can produce several
  Increments.
- The **Definition of Done** states the quality conditions completed work
  must satisfy; work not meeting it stays visible as unfinished.

## 9. The Sprint and its events

A **Sprint** is a fixed period of one month or less, containing planning,
development, inspection, and improvement.

| Event | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Sprint Planning** | the team defines Why (Sprint Goal), What (selected Product Backlog items), and How (the Developers' actionable plan); max 8 hours for a one-month Sprint |
| **Daily Scrum** | 15-minute daily event: inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal, adapt the plan for the day |
| **Sprint Review** | Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome and discuss what to do next |
| **Sprint Retrospective** | the team examines its own process — collaboration, tools, quality — and chooses useful changes to how it works |

**Sprint Review vs Sprint Retrospective**:

| | Sprint Review | Sprint Retrospective |
|---|---|---|
| Main focus | product outcome and progress toward the Product Goal | development process, collaboration, quality |
| Participants | Scrum Team and relevant stakeholders | Scrum Team only |
| Adaptation | revises the direction and order of future product work | improves the team's way of working |

## 10. The integrated Scrum cycle

`Product Backlog / Product Goal` → `Sprint Planning` → `Sprint Backlog /
Sprint Goal` → `Development and Daily Scrum` → `Increment meets DoD` →
`Sprint Review (product and future work)` → `Sprint Retrospective
(development process)` → process improvements feed the next Sprint's
Planning, while the Review's findings feed the Product Backlog.

## To remember

- Plan-driven plans everything up front; agile plans near-term detail and
  revises as it learns, through frequent increments.
- Agile Manifesto: individuals/interactions, working software, customer
  collaboration, responding to change are valued *more* — not *instead of*
  their counterparts.
- Scrum's three accountabilities: **Product Owner** (value, backlog order),
  **Developers** (build the Increment), **Scrum Master** (coach, remove
  impediments) — self-managing, no hierarchy.
- Three artifacts, each with a commitment: Product Backlog ↔ Product Goal,
  Sprint Backlog ↔ Sprint Goal, Increment ↔ Definition of Done.
- Four Sprint events in order: **Planning → Daily Scrum (repeated) → Review →
  Retrospective**. Review looks at the *product*; Retrospective looks at the
  *process*.

questions.question_text: What does a product vision identify?
questions.choice_a: The exact source code structure of the first release
questions.choice_b: The proposed product, its users, and the value it should provide
questions.choice_c: Only the technical architecture, not the users
questions.choice_d: The final, unchangeable feature list
questions.explanation: A product vision identifies the proposed product, its users, and the value it provides; detailed features develop as the team learns more.

questions.question_text: In plan-driven development, when is planning mostly done?
questions.choice_a: Substantial requirements and design detail are defined before implementation
questions.choice_b: Only near-term detail is planned, revised as knowledge grows
questions.choice_c: Planning never happens, only coding
questions.choice_d: Planning happens exclusively during the Sprint Retrospective
questions.explanation: Plan-driven development defines substantial requirements and design detail up front, unlike agile which plans near-term detail and revises later work.

questions.question_text: What best describes agile development's approach to change?
questions.choice_a: Change is avoided entirely once planning is finished
questions.choice_b: Frequent increments are used to evaluate results and redirect work
questions.choice_c: Only the customer may request changes, and only once
questions.choice_d: Changes are batched and applied only at project end
questions.explanation: Agile development uses frequent increments to evaluate results and redirect work, embracing change as understanding grows.

questions.question_text: What is incremental development, as distinct from iterative development?
questions.choice_a: Revisiting and improving an existing result after evaluation
questions.choice_b: Extending the product with additional usable functionality that works with what already exists
questions.choice_c: Writing all requirements before any code
questions.choice_d: A synonym for the Sprint Retrospective
questions.explanation: Incremental development extends the product with additional usable functionality (Feature A -> A+B -> A+B+C); iterative development instead revisits and improves an existing result.

questions.question_text: According to the Agile Manifesto, which of these is valued MORE, without discarding the other side entirely?
questions.choice_a: Comprehensive documentation over working software
questions.choice_b: Working software over comprehensive documentation
questions.choice_c: Following a plan over responding to change
questions.choice_d: Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
questions.explanation: The manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation, while still recognizing documentation's value.

questions.question_text: Which of the five agile development principles is 'reduce unnecessary complexity in the software and in the development process'?
questions.choice_a: Embrace change
questions.choice_b: Focus on people
questions.choice_c: Maintain simplicity
questions.choice_d: Involve the customer
questions.explanation: Maintain simplicity means reducing unnecessary complexity in both the software and the process used to build it.

questions.question_text: Which Extreme Programming practice means writing a test for required behaviour before coding it?
questions.choice_a: Continuous integration
questions.choice_b: Refactoring
questions.choice_c: Small releases
questions.choice_d: Test-driven development
questions.explanation: Test-driven development writes a test for the required behaviour before coding, then reruns the tests after changes.

questions.question_text: Which XP practice improves code structure while preserving its externally observable behaviour?
questions.choice_a: Refactoring
questions.choice_b: Incremental planning
questions.choice_c: Continuous integration
questions.choice_d: Test-driven development
questions.explanation: Refactoring improves the internal structure of code without changing its externally observable behaviour.

questions.question_text: What does Scrum organize complex product development around?
questions.choice_a: A single long planning phase followed by one release
questions.choice_b: Short Sprints and regular inspection
questions.choice_c: Unlimited-length iterations with no fixed events
questions.choice_d: A fixed contract signed before any work begins
questions.explanation: Scrum organizes complex product development around short Sprints and regular inspection, with defined responsibilities, events, and artifacts.

questions.question_text: What are Scrum's three pillars of empiricism, and in what relationship?
questions.choice_a: Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation — each supports the next
questions.choice_b: Planning, Coding, Testing — done in sequence once
questions.choice_c: Product Owner, Developers, Scrum Master — a command hierarchy
questions.choice_d: Backlog, Sprint, Increment — three separate teams
questions.explanation: Empiricism rests on Transparency (visible work), Inspection (examine progress), and Adaptation (adjust when inspection reveals a problem); each pillar supports the next.

questions.question_text: Which of these is one of the five Scrum values?
questions.choice_a: Documentation
questions.choice_b: Courage
questions.choice_c: Contract negotiation
questions.choice_d: Hierarchy
questions.explanation: The five Scrum values are Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage.

questions.question_text: Which Scrum accountability is responsible for maximizing product value and keeping the Product Backlog ordered and understandable?
questions.choice_a: Scrum Master
questions.choice_b: Developers
questions.choice_c: Product Owner
questions.choice_d: Stakeholders
questions.explanation: The Product Owner maximizes product value, communicates product direction, and keeps the Product Backlog ordered and understandable.

questions.question_text: Which Scrum accountability creates a usable Increment and plans the Sprint's work?
questions.choice_a: Developers
questions.choice_b: Product Owner
questions.choice_c: Scrum Master
questions.choice_d: Project manager
questions.explanation: Developers create a usable Increment, plan the Sprint's work, uphold quality, and adapt the plan as development progresses.

questions.question_text: What does 'self-managing', as applied to a Scrum Team, mean?
questions.choice_a: The team follows strict orders from the Scrum Master
questions.choice_b: The team decides who does what, when, and how; the accountabilities do not form a command hierarchy
questions.choice_c: Only the Product Owner can assign tasks
questions.choice_d: Each Developer works entirely alone with no coordination
questions.explanation: Self-managing means the team itself determines who does what, when, and how, with no command hierarchy among Product Owner, Developers, and Scrum Master.

questions.question_text: Which commitment gives the Product Backlog a shared basis for understanding its longer-term direction?
questions.choice_a: Sprint Goal
questions.choice_b: Definition of Done
questions.choice_c: Product Goal
questions.choice_d: Sprint Backlog
questions.explanation: The Product Goal is the commitment attached to the Product Backlog, describing a future state the product should reach.

questions.question_text: Which commitment states the quality conditions completed product work must satisfy?
questions.choice_a: Sprint Goal
questions.choice_b: Definition of Done
questions.choice_c: Product Goal
questions.choice_d: Sprint Backlog
questions.explanation: The Definition of Done states the quality conditions completed work must meet before it contributes to an Increment.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum length of a Sprint?
questions.choice_a: One week
questions.choice_b: One month or less
questions.choice_c: Three months
questions.choice_d: There is no maximum
questions.explanation: A Sprint is a fixed period of one month or less, containing planning, development, inspection, and improvement.

questions.question_text: What three questions does Sprint Planning address?
questions.choice_a: Who, When, Where
questions.choice_b: Why (Sprint Goal), What (selected items), How (the plan)
questions.choice_c: What, When, Budget
questions.choice_d: How much, How long, Who pays
questions.explanation: Sprint Planning addresses Why (the Sprint Goal), What (Product Backlog items selected), and How (the Developers' actionable delivery plan).

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?
questions.choice_a: A 15-minute daily event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan
questions.choice_b: A monthly status report to management
questions.choice_c: The event where the Product Backlog is created from scratch
questions.choice_d: A one-time kickoff meeting at the start of the whole project
questions.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers on every working day of the Sprint, inspecting progress and adjusting the plan for the day.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes the Sprint Review from the Sprint Retrospective in main focus?
questions.choice_a: Review focuses on the product outcome; Retrospective focuses on the development process
questions.choice_b: Review focuses on the process; Retrospective focuses on the product
questions.choice_c: They have exactly the same focus and participants
questions.choice_d: Review is for the Scrum Master only; Retrospective is for stakeholders only
questions.explanation: The Sprint Review inspects the product outcome and progress toward the Product Goal, with stakeholders present; the Retrospective examines the team's own process, with only the Scrum Team.

questions.question_text: Who participates in the Sprint Retrospective?
questions.choice_a: The Scrum Team and relevant stakeholders
questions.choice_b: Stakeholders only
questions.choice_c: The Scrum Team only
questions.choice_d: The Product Owner alone
questions.explanation: Unlike the Sprint Review, which includes stakeholders, the Sprint Retrospective involves only the Scrum Team, examining its own collaboration, tools, and quality.

exercises.prompt: Which Scrum accountability is responsible for coaching the team, establishing Scrum, and helping remove impediments to progress?
exercises.explanation: The Scrum Master helps establish Scrum, improves team effectiveness, coaches the team, and helps remove impediments to progress.

exercises.prompt: What is the name of the commitment attached to the Sprint Backlog, expressing one Sprint's shared objective?
exercises.explanation: The Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog: the shared outcome the team seeks for that Sprint.

exercises.prompt: Order the events that occur within a single Sprint.
steps: Sprint Planning — the team defines the Sprint Goal, selects Product Backlog items, and plans the work
Development and Daily Scrum, repeated on every working day — inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the day's plan
Sprint Review — the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome and discuss what to do next
Sprint Retrospective — the Scrum Team examines its own process and chooses useful changes to how it works
exercises.explanation: A Sprint always opens with Planning, is filled with Development punctuated by the Daily Scrum, and closes with the Review (product-focused) followed by the Retrospective (process-focused).

exercises.prompt: Order the stages of the integrated Scrum cycle, from the Product Backlog to the next Sprint's Planning.
steps: Product Backlog / Product Goal — the ordered, evolving list of work and its longer-term direction
Sprint Planning — selects items and defines the Sprint Backlog / Sprint Goal
Development and Daily Scrum — Developers build toward an Increment that meets the Definition of Done
Sprint Review — inspects the product and informs the Product Backlog for the next cycle
Sprint Retrospective — inspects the development process and produces improvements for the next Sprint
exercises.explanation: Product decisions shape the Sprint; the Sprint produces an Increment; the Review feeds insights back into the Product Backlog, while the Retrospective's process improvements carry into the next Sprint's Planning.

exercises.prompt: Build the flowchart of one increment of incremental development: select features, refine them, implement and test, integrate and test the system, then deliver and evaluate, with feedback looping back to the next selection.
exercises.hint: Linear process chain of five steps, then loop back from the last step to the first (no decision node needed  it always loops).
exercises.explanation: Each increment selects a manageable set of features, refines and implements them, integrates and tests the whole, then delivers and evaluates — feedback from evaluation informs the next selection, so the cycle loops rather than ending.

exercises.prompt: Which pair of artifact and commitment is correctly matched?
exercises.explanation: Each artifact has one commitment: Product Backlog ↔ Product Goal, Sprint Backlog ↔ Sprint Goal, Increment ↔ Definition of Done.
